articles.title: DOJ issues new subpoenas in Alaska Senate probe
articles.summary: The Justice Department has begun issuing a new wave of subpoenas stemming from an ongoing criminal investigation into Alaska's U.S. Senate race, multiple sou...
articles.body:
The Justice Department has begun issuing a new wave of subpoenas stemming from an ongoing criminal investigation into Alaska's Senate race, including the alleged efforts by Democrats to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, multiple sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News.

The subpoenas are targeting several Democratic officials believed to be tied to the effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to appear on Alaska's ballot. Nobody involved in the race has been charged with a crime.

The department also amended its civil lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Sullivan loses due to "voter confusion," adding in details from a New York Times report on alleged efforts by people associated with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign to find candidates who could draw votes away from Sullivan. The new filing calls the situation a "conspiracy to undermine the integrity of the electoral process."

Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied any connection to the effort to put Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel S. Sullivan has said in the past he is genuinely interested in running.

During a briefing with reporters Thursday, a Justice Department official offered perspective into the department's investigative approach in its criminal probe, saying there had been a "significant increase in activity" surrounding the Alaska race over the previous 24 hours. The Times report was published on Wednesday.

The Times' article detailed internal emails and text messages from individuals with knowledge of the alleged recruitment efforts — information the official suggested might significantly expand the government's ability to pursue its criminal investigation, since such communications are historically difficult for investigators to obtain without search warrants or voluntary cooperation from individuals with access to the material.

The official also alluded to possible investigative steps, like preservation requests to technology companies, search warrants for electronic communications and grand jury subpoenas seeking documents or testimony from those allegedly involved.

Asked what federal crimes could be implicated by an alleged recruitment scheme, the Justice Department official identified two civil rights statutes, 18 U.S.C. Sections 241 and 242, as potential roads for prosecutorial action.

Section 241 prohibits conspiracies to interfere with federally protected rights, including voting rights, while section 242 centers on willful deprivation of rights under color of law. The official added that prosecutors might, in a situation like this, examine whether there was a coordinated effort to trick voters into selecting a candidate.

The official referenced the federal prosecution of Douglass Mackey, convicted of conspiracy for posting misleading messages online during the 2016 election falsely encouraging Hillary Clinton supporters to vote by text message. That conviction was ultimately overturned by a federal appeals court in 2025.

Still, a Justice Department official acknowledged that the agency was not aware of any confirmed instances in which an Alaska voter had mistakenly cast a ballot for the wrong Dan Sullivan.

"I think I've not heard of that, but it's hard to tell exactly," the official said when asked whether voters had reported confusion or attempted to correct their ballots.

Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy directed a separate state investigation this week , ordering Alaska's Department of Public Safety to examine whether the alleged recruitment effort violated state law and whether criminal or civil action is merited.

CBS News has reached out to the Department of Justice, Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for comment.

The criminal investigation is ramping up alongside a separate civil lawsuit filed by the Trump administration last week, seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying the Senate election results under certain circumstances if the Republican incumbent loses.

That lawsuit addresses the government's concerns that votes intended for Sen. Sullivan could instead go to Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whose candidacy was previously challenged by state election officials but ultimately greenlit by Alaska's Supreme Court .

The suit, which argues Sullivan's candidacy violates the National Voter Registration Act, was amended on Thursday to include the Times' reporting. It now includes a second claim for relief, arguing the court needs to intervene under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause in order to allow the government to enforce the law and prevent a "conspiracy."

"Although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief. It also aligns with common sense," the amended complaint reads.

Alaska officials have previously asked a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that election administration is a state responsibility.

During Thursday's briefing, before the suit was amended, Justice Department officials largely characterized the civil lawsuit as an effort to preserve the government's ability to challenge an election result if deemed necessary.

"I don't see this as much more than a preservation suit," one official offered, arguing that once ballots are counted and separated from envelopes, establishing whether individual voters were confused becomes increasingly challenging.

The official also expressed interest in obtaining discovery concerning what Peltola's campaign knew about the alleged recruitment operation, and furthermore, when campaign officials may have learned of it.

President Trump has railed against the Alaska ballot situation, calling for Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan to be taken off the ballot. Asked by reporters about the Justice Department's lawsuit, he said last week: "Well, I'm the one that said, 'Do it.'"

articles.title: A ghost story in the US Capitol
articles.summary: Chad Pergram recalls slipping on the U.S. Capitol steps in front of Justin Trudeau and explores the ghostly history behind his unexpected fall.
articles.body: They always ask if I felt something. "Across your foot? Your shin?" My shin? "Yeah. Your ankle. Did you feel it?" Not really. But before I respond, they ask again. What was it like?" they inquired. "Or did you just fall?" Then they speculated I might be clumsy. Hmmph. Clumsy. I truly don’t think so. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS BRACES FOR POST-ELECTION GAME OF MUSICAL CHAIRS AS LEADERSHIP BATTLES LOOM Oh. I fall like everyone else. I work out daily. I’ve taken a couple of tumbles on predawn runs in Alexandria, Virginia. You never know when one of those sidewalk snakes will slither up from the asphalt and nip you on the ankle. I used to snow ski. I studied martial arts for years and hold a second degree black belt. Clumsy? Nah. "But, what do you think it was?" they follow up. Well, I have my theories. I was a little tired that day. I noted the lip on the small staircase near the Memorial Door of the U.S. Capitol where I may have caught the edge of my brown loafers. I remember my shoes. Rubber soles. Slight scuff on the toes. Perfectly matched with my crisp tan summer suit. Not quite an "Obama" tan suit. But appropriate for summer. And I thought at least reasonably dapper for traipsing around the U.S. Capitol and covering Congress on a sweltering July day. Was it the shoes? My fatigue? Or how about my haste to "get the story." I spotted then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and his small coterie of aides and a security detail descending a spiral staircase after a meeting with then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. D-Calif. I would try to ask Trudeau a question. No. This really doesn’t have anything to do with Trudeau. Or the fact that I recalled that there was a picture of him, aged about 14 or 15, at Olympic Stadium in Montreal, rooting for the Expos. He’s there with his father — the most storied of all Canadian prime ministers — the late Pierre Trudeau. Of course, the Expos no longer play in Montreal. They don’t play at all. They moved to Washington in 2005 and are now the Nationals. And this was before the tariff wars. Montreal has been bereft of Major League Baseball ever since. What would Youppi! Say? Look him up, kids. No, there wasn’t something across my shin or ankle. I didn’t feel anything. I was there, on those steps, in the U.S. Capitol, because I’m a baseball fan. And I found out that Justin Trudeau watched those old Montreal Expos teams in the 1980s. Stocked with Andre Dawson, Warren Cromartie and Steve Rogers. And even though Trudeau was there to discuss affairs of state with Pelosi and others, I was there to ask him about the national pastime. Ironic, I know, to pose such an interrogative to a Canadian. However, the reason was that there was a report that the Tampa Bay Rays might consider splitting their season each year between Florida and Montreal. Big league baseball would return to Quebec. It would be international news if Trudeau commented. It would appear on Fox. FS1. ESPN. TSN in Canada. And Montreal — famously robbed of perhaps winning the World Series in 1994 with the best team in the game that year because of the player’s strike — might have a shot again at baseball glory. But journalism is like baseball. A game of failure. You sometimes swing and miss. You’re doing great if you’re successful three out of ten times. THE HITCHHIKER'S GUIDE TO WHY REMOVING ILHAN OMAR FROM CONGRESS COULD BE HARDER THAN TRUMP EXPECTS And sometimes, in journalism, the question is never asked. That was this day. On those steps. Questions about the Rays and Montreal were muted. All because of whatever got me. Absolutely got me. I stepped toward Trudeau, mumbled something about Tampa Bay and bought it. I fell on those steps. Directly in front of the Canadian Prime Minister. On the hard Capitol marble. I quickly realized I was about to fall. With a microphone in one hand, I couldn’t catch myself. I was confident I’d break a wrist or a hand if I tried to catch myself. So, I just went with it and fell. And because I studied martial arts for all of those years from Master Kim and Master Yang back at the Tae Kwon Do dojang, I knew how to fall without hurting myself. I rolled onto my right shoulder toward Trudeau. My feeling flew up absurdly high in the air. "Oh Chad! Oh Chad! Oh Chad!" hollered my photographer, Robert Fetzer. "Chad!" Trudeau stopped briefly. But I leaped to my feet after the roll, hoping he might say something about baseball. I struck out. And Trudeau departed. "But what tripped you?" they ask. "Were you all right?" Physically, I was fine. Mentally, kind of garbled. I’ve worked daily at the U.S. Capitol for decades. I had a sneaking suspicion of what got me. Or better yet, who? In the latter years of the 19th Century, Rep. William Taulbee, D-Ky., did not get along with reporter Charles Kincaid. Taulbee thought Kincaid wasn’t an honest broker, writing screeds about his personal affairs. Taulbee was tall, towering over the diminutive Kincaid. Taulbee was known to sometimes physically pummel Kincaid. Taulbee was out of federal office. But Kincaid knew Taulbee would be at the Capitol. Kincaid packed a pistol with him. And on Feb. 28, 1890, the reporter shot the Bluegrass Congressman square in the eye. Taulbee leaked blood all the way down the House’s "Y" staircase, the plasma blending with marble. Through a miracle of chemistry, the splotches are still visible today. The Kentucky Democrat succumbed to his injuries 11 days later. It probably goes without saying that Taulbee does not like the congressional press corps. And, so, his phantasm is known to lurk around the Capitol. Sometimes low bridging reporters on ornate staircases. "What tripped you?" they ask. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP And before I can answer, my inquisitors jump to a conclusion, albeit an interrogative one. "Was it a ghost?" they giddily exclaim, like they had just figured out Final Jeopardy. As I say, I have my theories. I’ll let you come to your own conclusions. But I don’t want to trip you up.

articles.title: US scraps G20 photo after European diplomats object to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
articles.summary: ATLANTA (AP) — The top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies opened two days of meetings in Atlanta on Friday after European objections to R...
articles.body:
ATLANTA (AP) — The top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies opened two days of meetings in Atlanta on Friday after European objections to Russia's participation forced the U.S. to cancel a photo of the foreign ministers, underscoring deep rifts among the group over global crises .

Secretary of State Marco Rubio pulled the plug on the traditional group photo after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that usually helps kick off such diplomatic gatherings. But he still opened the talks, which otherwise went ahead as planned, with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.

"We are in a critical moment — I would call it a moment of choosing, and I would say not just for my country, the United States of America, but frankly, for the world," Rubio told his colleagues.

"We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises," he added, pointing to disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation. Many are posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order."

Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to consensus on many of the most contentious issues they face. Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran , U.S. tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea . All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade.

Russia's presence at G20 gathering roils European allies

Concerns about any prospects for the talks escalated when the Europeans balked at being photographed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Rubio decided to scrap the picture because he thought the controversy would be a distraction, according to two U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.

Some G20 countries had already expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.

The British foreign office said in a statement that the United Kingdom "has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that."

Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said the cancellation of the group photo was "the right decision" by the U.S., telling media in Atlanta that "I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov."

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said "there is no normality with Russia" but "we must exchange the controversies at the table here," the German news agency dpa reported. He added that "we also must not send falsely optimistic signals."

Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow. His presence in Atlanta could cause domestic political problems for Trump just days before the U.S. congressional midterm elections as well as roil the G20, according to Ian Kelly, a U.S. ambassador to Georgia during Trump's first term.

"It seems politically boneheaded to invite him," said Kelly, who now teaches international relations and diplomacy at Northwestern University outside Chicago.

The meeting in Atlanta is meant to set the stage for a G20 leaders' summit hosted by President Donald Trump at his Miami golf club in December. It is unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump's invitation to that gathering.

Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as U.S. officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group.

But missing from the invite list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top U.S. officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.

"We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary," said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.

Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate "on an equal footing with other members" when Britain takes over the presidency next year.

The U.S. has said a top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz , the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea. The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors.

But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge.

The Associated Press has reported that U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections and the possibility that Iran will retaliate against them.

Associated Press writers Michelle Gumede in Johannesburg, South Africa, Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, Geir Moulson in Berlin, Jill Lawless in London and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed.

articles.title: 'It could be quite a brutal evening': GOP braces for some once-unthinkable losses
articles.summary: Some GOP incumbents are still begging for more money in the final stretch.
articles.body:
Republicans are bracing for a brutal election night, convinced they're set to face some previously unthinkable losses in deep-red Trump territory as key battleground races hang on a knife's edge .

House Republicans are privately discussing not just if they'll lose their majority, but by how many seats. Imperiled GOP incumbents in once safe districts have been begging party leaders for more money in the final few days to stem the bleeding, according to six people involved in internal conversations, granted anonymity to discuss them. Senate Republicans have found new cause to worry about contests in Ohio, Kansas and other red states.

"It could be quite a brutal evening," said one senior Republican involved in the private conversations, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. "Once the dominoes start falling it becomes hard to stop them."

Some Republican incumbents made an eyebrow-raising emergency decision. They stopped doing their own polling weeks ago as they tried to save every dollar for swaying voters as they begged for the GOP cavalry to arrive from President Donald Trump's political operation to the National Republican Congressional Committee, according to three of the people.

One Republican strategist working on midterm races simply responded to a question about the environment with a video of a dumpster on fire that was being swept away by flood waters.

Top GOP officials and lawmakers have long known the political landscape would be bad, amid voter anger over the cost of living and aspects of Trump's policy agenda. But they're facing a worse position than they expected earlier this year, with less than one week until Election Day.

Republicans for weeks have worried that young men who'd voted for Trump, including white and Hispanic working class voters, will stay home amid disillusionment with high costs and the Iran war.

That alone could allow Democrats to overperform in some areas after they hemorrhaged support among that voting bloc in 2024.

At a Kwik Trip in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, this week in the hotly-contested 3rd District, Isaiah Romero was filling up his silver Ram truck. The 20-year-old said he cast his ballot for Trump in his first ever presidential election two years ago. His verdict on high fuel prices? "I think they're bull," he said as he looked over to the $6.39 per gallon diesel and $4.29 gas at the pump.

Is he voting this time? "No," Romero responded, adding: "I didn't vote for this."

New fires have been popping up across the map just as soon as top GOP officials put out others. Trump canceled in-person rallies in deep-red Kansas and Iowa set for this weekend to instead hold a series of tele-rallies for GOP candidates in the final stretch.

"Any Democrats telling you they aren't winning the Senate [besides] a couple of seats are sandbagging expectations," the senior Republican said.

In Ohio, the race between GOP Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is still incredibly close in private and public polling. But Republicans have watched with horror as GOP governor nominee "Vivek's [Ramaswamy's] numbers have gone off a cliff" in the last few days after he ran an ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother saying her daughter is a liar, according to the senior Republican and two others who saw the internal polling. Acton's stepfather was charged with raping her when she was 12.

The headwinds across all of Ohio are deeply problematic for Republicans. They now believe embattled Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) — who is facing child and domestic abuse allegations that he denies — will lose in a seat Trump won by double digits.

South Carolina has become another unexpectedly nailbiting race for Republicans, where political newcomer Sen. Darline Graham is facing a well-funded Democratic challenger. But GOP operatives and officials are feeling somewhat better after outside groups injected cash into the race earlier this month and Trump announced another rally in the state to energize Republicans' base.

"It's a lot closer than I think we would ever want, but I think she's going to pull it out," said Jeff Davis, chair of the Greenville County Republican Party.

But in one of the most dire signs, once-unimaginable GOP worries have started to creep about deep-red Louisiana — where Trump announced this week he will hold an election-eve tele-rally for Senate nominee Julia Letlow. Speaker Mike Johnson, who is close with Letlow, will join as Republicans have grown wary about a surge of Black voters and other Democratic-leaning voters in early voting across the South.

Senior Republicans believe Letlow will win, but they fear it will be by single digits if nothing changes.

"The cakewalk turned into a knife fight," said one Louisiana Republican who has talked with Letlow recently. "If Democrat turnout surges on Election Day, it'll be a long night in Monroe," the person added, and they expect Letlow to win by just 6 points in a state Trump won by 22 points two years ago.

In another painful development for Republicans in Louisiana, GOP groups have even started an eye-popping spending war in a safe red gerrymandered seat — where a bitter Republican-on-Republican primary is unfolding between state Sen. Blake Miguez, who was formerly endorsed by Trump , and state Sen. Rick Edmonds, Johnson's former pastor. Club for Growth poured another $220,000 into the race Thursday. Republicans fear the messy race is poised for a December runoff.

"POLITICO's sad little rolodex of loser strategists have no idea what they're talking about, and if they really believe what they're saying they should come out of the shadows and put a name to their brain-dead comments," said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre.

"While Republicans have focused on real solutions to improve costs of living and make our nation safer, Democrats have nominated a gang of radicals who want to raise taxes, force everyone on government healthcare, and release criminals onto the streets," said Joanna Rodriguez, spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

On the House side, Republicans are bracing for a brutal night. But they've long been spending in some redder GOP districts to forestall a true disaster.

Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, said that the committee worked in partnership with the campaigns and the RNC to launch coordinated advertising early in GOP-held districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (Colo.), Bill Huizenga (Mich.), Rob Wittman (Va.), Mike Turner (Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (Texas).

The NRCC began airing coordinated ads in early August, more than a month before the DCCC. The NRCC also conducted polling in more than 100 districts, an eye-popping number, as they worked to see how far the fires had spread into red terrain and make sure they were moving resources where they were needed.

Republicans still think they can unseat Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), while flipping retiring Rep. Jared Golden's (D-Maine) seat. But privately, Republicans believe North Carolina's open 11th District is close to gone, as are several other deep-red seats Trump won by double digits, according to four people with knowledge of the situation. And they're still not confident they'll beat Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) in a seat the GOP thought would be an easy flip when they redrew it early this year. It's become the most expensive House race in history.

The Republican in Kentucky's 6th district, where Trump won by 15 points in 2024, is barely hanging on, according to the four people.

Even in the South Texas districts the GOP redrew in their favor, Republicans reached the point days ago where no amount of new money is going to change the upcoming catastrophe, said one Republican official involved in conversations about those races.

Johnson traveled to Minnesota on Thursday to headline a fundraiser for GOP Rep. Brad Finstad, who Republicans are scrambling to shore up in a +12 Trump district. Finstad told POLITICO in an interview this week that he had warned senior Republicans for weeks about Democratic groups pouring money into the race in his southern Minnesota district.

"We raised that with anybody and everybody that would want to hear it," Finstad said. "From a global perspective, people were like, 'Well, you won by 18, you're fine.' And, you know, those of us in Minnesota know that this district has always had kind of an independent streak to it."

Senate Democrats, meanwhile, are upbeat at their prospects, but public and private polling across close to the entire battleground map is running within the margin of error — meaning those states could break either way.

"I would rather be us than them. But if anyone tells you they know what's going to happen, they're full of shit," one senior Senate Democratic operative said. "Everything is close."

And some Republicans are taking solace in the fact that at least it'll all soon be over.

"I can see the light at the end of the tunnel," said a GOP strategist working on a campaign that is trending toward Democrats. "It might be a semi-truck, but at least I can see it."

Andrew Howard, Erin Doherty and Alec Hernández contributed to this report.

articles.title: Lawyers for ex-FBI Director James Comey will ask a judge to block Justice Department prosecution
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Lawyers for former FBI Director James Comey will ask a federal judge on Friday to block the Justice Department from pursuing its third crim...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Lawyers for former FBI Director James Comey will ask a federal judge on Friday to block the Justice Department from pursuing its third criminal case against the outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and frequent target of Republican outrage.

Court documents unsealed Monday showed that the Trump administration this month bypassed a grand jury and filed a charging document known as a "criminal information" over allegations of a decade-old and previously investigated news media leak. The Justice Department defended the maneuver as an effort to extend the legal time limit for seeking a grand jury indictment, but Comey's lawyers have called the case legally invalid.

U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden, a Trump nominee, was expected to hear arguments on that question Friday.

The effort to prosecute Comey, who says he is innocent of the allegations, is part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections .

Comey was fired by Trump in May 2017 as he oversaw an investigation into whether Trump's presidential campaign conspired with Russia to tip the 2016 election in his favor over Democrat Hillary Clinton. The two men have been bitterly at odds since, with Comey likening Trump to a corrupt mafia don in a book he published and the president accusing him of treason and calling for his imprisonment.

The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of lying to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed.

A separate pending indictment charges Comey with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47" — 86 is slang meaning "to throw out," "to get rid of" or "to refuse service to," and Trump is the 47th president. The former FBI director has sought to dismiss the case.

"Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement Monday after the documents were unsealed. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice — one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."

The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.

Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI's conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey's attorneys said in a recent court filing.

In 2019, the U.S. attorney's office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name "Tropical Vortex." But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in early 2020.

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: A guide to knowing who won by bedtime

articles.body:
Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. EDT as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in!

The general premise of this note is that normal people want to follow politics, too. OK, maybe “need” is a better word, since wanting to follow politics closely these days would be a sure marker of abnormality.

There are a lot of places where you can go to get a constant transfusion of all the contradictory conjecture, spin, scooplet and data drops that your heart desires. But why do that, when you can pay us to do it for you? We comb through the minutiae and then, taking a longer, broader view, offer you a primer in the hope that we can discard some debris and, with respect for your time and attention, give you a weekly rundown of what’s happening.

This is our last note before the end of a midterm election cycle that began in earnest last spring when Texas kicked off a gerrymandering war, then intensified with off-year contests in Virginia and New Jersey, and then roared into a wild-and-wooly primary season in early 2026.

We’ve been offering you polling averages on President Trump ’s job approval rating and national voters’ preferences for partisan control of Congress. In our final, preelection tabulation we find the president at 34.6 percent, down 6 points from a year ago, and the preference for Democratic control at 52 percent, up 4.8 points from a year ago.

For some basic framing, just imagine that someone told you a year ago that those numbers would have moved in those directions by those amounts. Given the GOP bloodbath that was taking place in Virginia and New Jersey, you’d figure that the midterms would be pretty rough for Republicans. And you would have been right.

For a lot of reasons relating to the gaming of expectations, intraparty positioning, looming presidential nomination contests and the political media’s tendency to build and then break narratives, it feels like the midterm climate has been full of wild swings. But if you skipped the previous 11 months and tuned in for the season finale, you would have missed some truly wild story arcs and crazy characters, but you would certainly know the plot.

Elections are wonderful things. There’s the pageant of democracy and the power of the people to fire their leaders. But there’s also the beautiful quality of their ending . We’ve lived in a world of “the permanent campaign” for decades, but the conclusion of elections, thank God, offers a pause. The people have spoken and everybody has to like it or lump it. The next cycle begins almost at once, but the reality benders of politics and media are, for a time at least, obliged to reset their spin cycles.

How well or poorly you think the parties do next week will mostly depend on your own allegiances. Democrats will be disappointed if they don’t score upsets in several deep-red states, and Republicans will be cheered if they manage to hang on in some places that the president won by more than a dozen points two years ago. Partisanship, it is rightly said, is a hell of a drug.

Now, we want you to stay up all night, glued to your television watching special coverage from NewsNation and the latest race calls from our partners at Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). While you’re at it, keep refreshing The Hill, clicking with wild abandon on the latest returns. You could rewatch old Whole Hog Politics videos on YouTube on a third screen. And as you stare, bleary-eyed at me, even blearier-eyed, at 2 a.m. EST as we wait for inklings from Alaska’s Mat-Su Valley you can feel that you are truly one with the great demos of the United States.

Or, maybe you have a job. Perhaps you have children who would like breakfast at 7 o’clock in the morning, regardless of how gripping you found the mail-in ballots from Idaho. We’ve got you covered.

We’re going to know a great deal about how the election went by 8 p.m., and by 10 p.m., it’s probably going to be all over but the shouting. We know this for a couple of reasons. First, how the votes are counted doesn’t have anything to do with how they are cast. About half of all ballots will have been submitted prior to Election Day. By that evening, as the polls are starting to close, we will be down to just a handful of stragglers. When you’re watching election coverage, you’re watching an unboxing of a completed product, not the creation of something new.

Second, similar voters tend to vote similarly. We are a wildly diverse continental republic that comprises a dizzying array of cultures and characters. But, with a profoundly nationalized form of politics these days, demographically similar voters in one part of the country tend to behave in similar ways, i.e., married white women with college degrees in Georgia may tend to be more Republican than their counterparts in Washington state, but history tells us that they will swing in similar directions by similar amounts.

Indeed, the country as a whole tends to swing one way or another. There will be some exceptions, and different regions will move more than others, but there will be a theme to the pudding next week. And, luckily, we will get a good taste of what’s happening even before primetime begins as states on the East Coast and in the Midwest start reporting their returns.

How much we will be able to say about the final disposition of the fight for the Senate and the House will depend on how big the swing is. If it’s a bigger blue wave than expected or if Republicans have rallied and rebuilt their red wall, we will be able to draw a lot of conclusions by, say, 8:30 p.m. Conversely, if the polling has been reliable and many of these races really are very close, we’re going to have to wait at least another hour before we get a sense of where the sea of ballots is going to crest.

With that in mind, we’re offering you the Whole Hog Politics guide to the first half of election night, or, if you like, how to sound like a pro to your family and friends even if you actually have a life.

After the jump, we’re going to lay out the poll closings in Eastern Standard Time from 6 p.m. until 9 p.m. We’ll offer you a guide to key races and, crucially, key counties that will tell us how voters are moving. While others are fuming at a graphic that is stuck at “72 percent of expected votes counted,” you’ll be able to zoom in on bellwether counties to see what’s likely to happen in the states and races as a whole.

So, save this email, and, on Tuesday, when you fire up the flatscreen and pass the pork rinds, you’ll be ahead of the game. And when your eyelids get heavy, you can go to bed with a pretty good idea of what you’ll be waking up to, other than a request for sliced bananas in the oatmeal.

Thanks for riding along with us this cycle. We’ll be back next week to tell you what we actually learned from voters and what it means going forward. Happy viewing!

articles.title: Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a US general election
articles.summary: VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pontiff to vote in a U. general election, casting a mail-in ballot in a contest that will decide Americ...
articles.body:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pontiff to vote in a U.S. general election, casting a mail-in ballot in a contest that will decide America's political future as the Trump era slowly comes to an end.

The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in the city ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections , citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.

Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen" as he has done "whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said.

The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru, where he lived as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years.

"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," it added.

Leo holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship , and is also the head of state of a foreign country, the Holy See. The city-state is an absolute monarchy with no political elections.

U.S. federal law allows citizens living abroad, even those working for foreign governments, to vote via absentee ballot. Americans working for foreign governments aren't automatically at risk of forfeiting their U.S. citizenship, though the U.S. State Department says on its website that it may "actively review" the citizenship status of Americans who "serve as a foreign head of state, foreign head of government, or foreign minister."

This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they're also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin's retirement. There are no statewide issues on the Illinois ballot. President Donald Trump is not on the ballot, but he has campaigned hard to try to preserve Republican control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of his second term.

The pope, registered at a New Lenox, Illinois, address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3, said Kim Fladhammer, chief of staff to the Will County clerk, on Friday. The Chicago Sun-Times first reported the request.

The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17.

It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope's older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude's, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.

Prevost's past votes have gone Democratic and Republican

Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.

The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.

While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.

The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.

Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants, following the Trump administration's crackdown and mass deportation program.

Earlier this year, Trump called Leo "weak" and captive to the "radical left," kicking off a remarkable back-and-forth public argument that dominated Leo's April trip to Africa.

Responding to Trump, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria: "I'm not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for."

The public dispute has subsided in recent months.

"We try to let things pass if there are misunderstandings," the Vatican foreign minister, Archbishop Richard Paul Gallagher, told reporters this week. "With anybody, we would be looking to approach it and say, 'OK, there may be a misunderstanding, let's move on and try to rebuild trust and confidence.'"

Leo and Trump have not spoken by phone since the pope's May 2025 election. Last week, however, Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the humanitarian crisis in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

Asked why Trump and Leo haven't spoken, Gallagher said the Holy See has found a capable conduit in the U.S. ambassador to the Holy See, Brian Burch, and hadn't needed to elevate any issue higher.

Leo has made clear on several occasions that he follows local and national U.S. politics closely and is not afraid to intervene.

Recently, Leo reiterated official church teaching declaring the death penalty "inadmissible." He made the pronouncement in a social media post on the World Day Against the Death Penalty, which came as the U.S. announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad . The plans were later scrapped.

In 2025, Leo intervened in a debate over abortion, after Chicago Cardinal Blase Cupich announced plans to give a lifetime achievement award to Sen. Durbin. The plans drew objection from some conservative U.S. bishops given the powerful Democratic senator's support for abortion rights. Leo called for respect for both sides, but he also pointed out the contradiction between people who call themselves "pro-life" but also support the death penalty.

Also in 2025, Leo said he was "very disappointed" that his home state of Illinois approved a law allowing medically assisted dying, which is condemned by the Catholic Church.

The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, in a note commenting on the confirmation of Leo's midterm vote, urged Catholics to put "our faith before our politics" and uphold human dignity and the common good.

"As Catholics and Americans, we are blessed to be able to participate in our nation's political and public life," said the conference's director of public affairs, Chieko Noguchi. "In voting, our Holy Father sets the example that encourages each citizen to exercise their civic responsibility."

Associated Press writers Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee, and Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrats hold 10-point lead over GOP in battle for Congress: Poll
articles.summary: Democrats have a 10-point lead over Republicans on a generic congressional ballot, as the parties face off for control of Congress in next week’s midterm election. An Emerson College Polling survey released Friday found Democrats broadly leading with 52 percent support over 42 percent support for the GOP. This is only slightly tighter than Democrats’…
articles.body:
Democrats have a 10-point lead over Republicans on a generic congressional ballot, as the parties face off for control of Congress in next week’s midterm election.

An Emerson College Polling survey released Friday found Democrats broadly leading with 52 percent support over 42 percent support for the GOP. This is only slightly tighter than Democrats’ 11-point lead in the polling center’s September survey .

The Democratic Party is fighting to retake control of both chambers of Congress this November. Decision Desk HQ’s forecast on Thursday put their odds of gaining control of the House at 80 percent and their chance of gaining majority power in the Senate at 60 percent.

Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, noted that support for Republicans is ending at the same 42 percent support level they began at in July 2025, when the polling center began tracking generic ballot support for this election cycle.

“Democratic support climbed eight points over the past fifteen months from 44% to 52%, undecided and swing voters clearly shifting in the Democrats’ favor,” Kimball said in a statement. “With about 5% still undecided, most of whom are independent and half disapprove of Trump, Democrats’ congressional ceiling could be higher than the poll reports.”

Kimball also noted President Trump’s plummeting approval ratings this year amid his administration’s ongoing military operations against Iran and a trade fight with Canada.

Fifty-seven percent of respondents in the October poll said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of his job as president — a 6-point increase since January. His approval rating was down to 37 percent in this new poll.

The survey also displayed an enthusiasm gap between Democrats and Republicans about voting in the upcoming midterms. Ninety-two percent of Democrats said they were either “very” or “somewhat” excited to cast their ballot in this election, while 85 percent of Republicans said the same.

The Emerson College Polling survey was conducted Oct. 24-26 among a sample of 1,000 likely voters with a margin of error of approximately 3 percentage points.

articles.title: The self-inflicted chaos of Missouri’s congressional elections
articles.summary: Politics may be a game, but the law is definitely not. Getting too cute in court almost always blows up in your face.
articles.body:
From midterm redistricting to pre-emptively attempting to prevent the certification of Alaska’s Senate election — providing, of course, that the “wrong” candidate wins — Republicans have been playing stupid electoral games. Now, at least in Missouri, they are about to collect their stupid prize.

Missouri has eight House seats . Currently, they are held by six Republicans and two Democrats. Through redistricting , Republicans thought they could gerrymander their way into an extra seat by redrawing five of them.

But there were problems. Missouri law requires a new congressional map be placed on hold once a successful referendum petition is filed. On Dec. 9, 2025, the group People, Not Politicians filed a referendum petition along with more than enough signatures to validate it. Instead of processing it, Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins sat on it for nine months. He then rejected it on the last possible day, on the bogus theory that the new maps couldn’t be the subject of a referendum under Missouri’s constitution.

The referendum filing kicked off a legal battle, with the Missouri Supreme Court eventually ruling unanimously that the new map could not be used and, in fact, had never been legal. In the meantime, however, Hoskins had sought to create “facts on the ground” by using the new map for the primary election and then arguing that it wouldn’t be constitutional to hold a primary election with one set of geographical congressional districts and the general election with another.

Various federal courts agreed that such an election would violate the Constitution, culminating in an opinion by the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals ordering the general election to use the same congressional map as the primaries did. But the U.S. Supreme Court stayed those orders three different times . So on Tuesday, Missouri will elect its House delegation based on the old map even though the candidates standing in that election won primaries based on the new one.

This next part gets slightly into the legal weeds, so stick with me. The U.S. Supreme Court didn’t actually decide the case on the merits. Rather, it stayed the Eighth Circuit’s order, allowing Hoskins to hold the election using the new map. It did so for a variety of technical legal reasons that had everything to do with the timing and posture of the case and nothing to do with whether it is actually constitutional to hold a general election using different congressional districts than were used in the primaries. But the court left the opinion itself in place.

What we are left with is an unprecedented legal train wreck. While Hoskins was not able to force Missouri to use the new congressional map in the general election, he did manage to get a published decision from a federal appellate court holding that conducting a general election using the old map violates the U.S. Constitution. This decision is currently good law and is binding in both federal and state courts.

In other words, once the election is over, Democrats can go to court, cite this opinion, and demand that the results of the election in the affected congressional districts not be certified. And their demand ought to be summarily granted.

That means that no representatives from at least five Missouri House districts will be able to take their seats in the new Congress, resulting in a net loss of probably three Republican seats rather than a gain of one, which was what Republicans were trying to pull off when this whole mess started.

The only way to really fix this is to hold new elections, a process that will take months. It’s doubtful that the Supreme Court would be able to intervene by the time the Congress convenes on Jan. 3 even if it wanted to. For one thing, there’s not enough time; the case would have to work its way through the state courts first. And if the Missouri Supreme Court found that the election also violated the state constitution, the U.S. Supreme Court could not intervene.

Of course, it is always possible that Democrats, out of some misguided notion of “fair play,” will refuse to pull the trigger and block the results from being certified. This would be an enormous mistake. If bad behavior never has consequences, then you get more bad behavior. Hoskins’s job as secretary of state was ensuring that Missouri has fair and free elections. Instead, he engaged in some of the most cynical, undemocratic behavior imaginable and ended up disenfranchising an entire state.

Politics may be a game, but the law is definitely not. Principles are principles and, once they are established, they can be used by either side. Getting too cute in court almost always blows up in your face.

That’s what happened here. In an effort to game the system for Republicans, Hoskins went to court and won a judgement preemptively declaring Missouri’s November congressional election to be unconstitutional and, therefore, uncertifiable. If Missouri can’t send House members to Congress, he and his Republican friends have no one to blame but themselves.

So let Republicans collect the stupid prize they have won. Hoskins’s humiliation will serve as a warning that no matter how foolishly our politicians behave, democracy is always a serious business.

Chris Truax is an appellate attorney and charter member of the Society for the Rule of Law.

articles.title: Hamilton holds slight lead over Marshall in Kansas Senate contest: Poll
articles.summary: Democrat Adam Hamilton is narrowly leading Republican Roger Marshall in the Kansas Senate race, according to a new poll. In the Emerson College Polling poll, 48.7 percent of respondents said they would cast their ballot or have already cast their ballot for Hamilton, while 45.2 percent said the same of Marshall. A Libertarian candidate garnered…
articles.body:
Democrat Adam Hamilton is narrowly leading Republican Roger Marshall in the Kansas Senate race, according to a new poll.

In the Emerson College Polling poll, 48.7 percent of respondents said they would cast their ballot or have already cast their ballot for Hamilton, while 45.2 percent said the same of Marshall. A Libertarian candidate garnered 2.9 percent support.

The credibility interval for the poll, comparable to a margin of error, is 3.5 points.

Hamilton’s lead as a Democrat in Kansas is notable, with the state having a reliably red history. Kansas hasn’t voted for a Democrat for president since the mid-1960s . The state also hasn’t elected a Democrat for Senate since the 1930s .

But the GOP is facing political headwinds this cycle in the form of the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval ratings and concerns about the cost of living. Amid the war, the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, has been closed, driving up energy costs.

In Kansas, a state with a notable agriculture sector, the price of diesel has risen from about $3.46 per gallon last year to about $6.05 per gallon as of Thursday afternoon, according to AAA. And the price of a regular gallon of gas in the state was at about $3.94, up from about $2.72 last year.

Both the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report and Decision Desk HQ rate the Hamilton-Marshall race as a “toss-up.”

In the Emerson College poll, 51 percent of respondents said they were against Trump’s job performance, while 44.9 percent were for it and 4.1 percent did not have an opinion.

The Emerson College poll took place from Oct. 26 to 28 and featured 800 likely voters in Kansas.

articles.title: Peltola denies knowing about Alaska spoiler candidate Dan J. Sullivan
articles.summary: Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola (D) on Thursday again denied knowing anything about her campaign’s alleged recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan to challenge her GOP opponent, incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), in an effort to dilute the incumbent’s vote share. “I just want to clear the air,” Peltola said during a speech in Juneau, Alaska,…
articles.body:
Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola (D) on Thursday again denied knowing anything about her campaign’s alleged recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan to challenge her GOP opponent, incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), in an effort to dilute the incumbent’s vote share.

“I just want to clear the air,” Peltola said during a speech in Juneau, Alaska, The Associated Press reported . “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent.”

She added, “That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

The high-stakes Senate race, which uses a ranked-choice system in Alaska, has made headlines in recent weeks after the Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a lawsuit claiming the presence of a candidate with the same name as the incumbent on the ballot could give Peltola an unfair advantage in the upcoming election.

On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the Democrat’s campaign was directly involved in recruiting the other Sullivan. Several GOP lawmakers took to social media to blast the Democratic candidate in the wake of the Times story.

“Alaskans will leave Peltola unranked on the ballot because of her dirty tricks. Voters can trust the real Dan Sullivan, and I’m confident he’ll be re-elected,” Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) wrote on the social platform X . He also called on the DOJ to investigate Peltola’s campaign.

“Two terms in Congress. Zero bills signed into law. But she found time to hunt down every Dan Sullivan in Alaska,” Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R) wrote online . “Let’s elect the REAL Dan Sullivan.”

President Trump, in a Truth Social post earlier this week, said the Alaska Democrat should face legal and political consequences.

“It has just been determined that the Democrats in Alaska illegally searched for, and recruited, a man named Dan Sullivan to run against our distinguished Republican Senator, Dan Sullivan, in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election, thereby taking votes away from the REAL Senator, Dan Sullivan,” Trump wrote.

The president has also said Peltola should not be allowed to run for Senate after the allegations.

Peltola’s campaign has also denied any involvement in the matter.

Outgoing Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) opened a probe into the alleged ballot stacking and said it could affect certification of the election should Peltola win next week. The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee also launched an investigation into the former lawmaker.

The race in Alaska is competitive, with nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ leaning narrowly in favor of Peltola, whom the forecaster gives 60 percent chance of winning.

articles.title: Cook Political Report shifts 12 more House races toward Democrats
articles.summary: The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, on Friday shifted a dozen more House races toward Democrats in the final stretch of the midterm cycle. The handicapper has shifted dozens of House races toward Democrats in recent weeks, and with the latest moves, it now forecasts more than 218 seats to “lean Democrat” or…
articles.body:
The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, on Friday shifted a dozen more House races toward Democrats in the final stretch of the midterm cycle.

The handicapper has shifted dozens of House races toward Democrats in recent weeks, and with the latest moves, it now forecasts more than 218 seats to “lean Democrat” or better, projecting a Democratic House majority of between 227 and 240 seats

Notable shifts include Colorado’s 5th Congressional District, represented by Rep. Jeff Crank (R), which moved from “lean Republican” to a “toss-up.” Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District, represented by Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R), and the open South Carolina 1st Congressional District made the same change.

Fitzpatrick serves in one of the only districts carried by former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

In her analysis, Cook House editor Erin Covey wrote the competitive Senate race in South Carolina between Democrat Annie Andrews and Sen. Darline Graham (R) may pull Democrats over the finish line — even in a district that Trump won by double digits two years ago.

“Currently, GOP outside groups are outspending Democrats by more than $3 million,” Covey said. “But some Republicans are still concerned it won’t be enough, particularly if Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews — a Charleston resident — carries this district by at least a couple of points.”

Another Pennsylvania district, the 8th Congressional District, was shifted from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat.” Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R) has trailed his Democratic opponent in recent polling, and Covey wrote that attacks over the lawmaker’s stock trades appear to be having an impact.

Ohio’s 9th District, represented by Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D), moved in the same direction. Republicans have twice redrawn Kaptur’s district in the GOP’s favor, but she has fended off challengers. The election handicapper forecasts she will once again come out on top next week.

Cook is also moving some safer Republican seats back onto the House battlefield, with Florida’s 7th and 9th congressional districts and Indiana’s 5th District moving from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican.”

“It’s clear that Spartz, who has faced serious primary challenges, is struggling to consolidate her base,” Covey wrote of Indiana Rep. Victoria Spartz (R). “Her own unpopularity, coupled with Trump’s sagging approval rating, puts this seat in contention.”

And moving from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” are North Carolina’s 5th and 9th congressional districts, New Jersey’s 2nd District and Washington’s 5th District — all districts that have GOP incumbents running for reelection.

Covey said that the wide margin in the Tar Heel State’s Senate race, where former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) leads ex-Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, may hurt Republicans even in some very red seats.

“Republicans, meanwhile, are deeply concerned about low turnout in North Carolina this cycle now that national GOP groups have stopped contesting the Senate race,” Covey added.

The shifts come as Republicans have pulled spending from some key House contests. Democrats only need to flip three seats for House control, making the GOP’s margin for error more slim.

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, is similarly bullish about Democrats in the House, giving the party an 80 percent chance of taking the majority.

articles.title: Unhinged judge who called Latino attorney a 'White savior' ordered to undergo psychiatric examination
articles.summary: Judge Ada Brown called attorney Ezra Young a "White savior" intimidated by "Black excellence" in a hearing now under Fifth Circuit investigation.
articles.body: A Trump-appointed judge was ordered to undergo a psychiatric examination as part of an ongoing judicial misconduct investigation after she called a Latino attorney a "White savior" who was intimidated by "Black excellence" due to his "White mediocrity" during a hearing. U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas, who is Black and Native American, was temporarily removed from her docket by the Fifth Circuit Judicial Council earlier this month, following a May judicial-conduct complaint filed by attorney Ezra Young, whose permission to practice before Brown had previously been revoked. The complaint centered on Brown's rhetoric toward Young during his appearance for a show-case hearing, in which he was facing sanctions over allegations from Brown that he shared sealed court filings online. Young represented a Black law professor who sued Southern Methodist University, alleging she was denied tenure because of discrimination. He joined the case in 2022 and appeared before Brown before the judge barred him from practicing in her courtroom. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORCHES TRUMP ADMIN IN LATEST COURTROOM SHOWDOWN, REFERS ATTORNEY FOR BAR REVIEW During the April hearing, Brown railed against Young, accusing him of "bullying" the Black attorneys on the case. "You’re the White savior, come to save all the stupid Black lawyers in Texas who need your help from New York," Brown later said, according to the transcript obtained by Bloomberg. Brown repeatedly brought attention to Young's skin color, calling him "White presenting" and "fair-skinned" after Brown told her that he was a Latino. "I think what’s happening here, quite candidly, is you are very intimidated for some reason, Mr. Young, with Black excellence, in light of your White mediocrity. Yeah. Right?" Brown said. "You should write that down. I mean, you — I’m — you look like a White man, right?" She also called Young a "Chad" which she said is the male version of "Karen." "It’s someone who calls the manager when they don’t get their way. They stomp their foot when the rules are supposed to apply to them, right?" Brown said. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE WITH TIES TO ANTI-TRUMP CONSPIRACY THEORY HIT WITH MISCONDUCT COMPLAINT Brown also accused Young of sensationalizing the case after reading a news article that quoted his brief and referenced another law professor’s comparison of the Black professor’s treatment in the tenure dispute to a "lynching." "And so when I read a headline — a sensationalized, very racialized headline that says, ‘it’s like I’ve been lynched,’ and it’s literally got no connection to this case, I have to ask you, Mr. Social Media, Main Character Chad, White Hero, Savior, Loves to Help Black People Be An Ally, where the lynching in this case came from?" Brown said. The release of the April court hearing transcripts comes as Brown shared with lawyers, judges and several media outlets via email of Young's complaint and her response. Meanwhile, in a July 28 filing responding to Young's complaint, Brown stood by her conduct. "I do not believe my demeanor was inappropriate at any time, especially during the candid conversations about race," Brown wrote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I take to heart the lessons I have learned from this experience and I ask the Chief Judge to weigh this candor, as well as my commitment to being mentored by senior judges with more experience in such situations when determining an appropriate disposition," Brown wrote. "I realize the importance of public confidence in the judiciary and take to heart my role in fostering the public’s faith in it." President Donald Trump appointed Brown to the federal court in Texas in March 2019. She is the first Black woman to serve in that court.

articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) issued dozens of subpoenas in connection with the ballot-stacking allegations against Alaska’s Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola.

On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was directly involved in recruiting someone with the same name as her opponent , Sen. Dan Sullivan (R). The presence of a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot prompted the DOJ earlier to file a lawsuit that claimed it gives an unfair advantage to the Alaska Democrat.

The latest subpoenas by the DOJ were sent to Peltola’s Senate campaign offices as well as the offices of Dan J. Sullivan, NBC News reported , citing a U.S. official. The Times also reported about the subpoenas, citing officials familiar with the investigation.

This comes after Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) ordered an investigation into whether Peltola’s campaign violated state law in the alleged scheme.

“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” the governor wrote in a social media post . “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”

The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee also launched an investigation into the Democratic lawmaker.

President Trump, in a Truth Social post on Wednesday, said the Alaska Democrat should face legal and political consequences.

“It has just been determined that the Democrats in Alaska illegally searched for, and recruited, a man named Dan Sullivan to run against our distinguished Republican Senator, Dan Sullivan, in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election, thereby taking votes away from the REAL Senator, Dan Sullivan,” the president wrote.

Peltola, on Thursday, denied any knowledge of the alleged ballot-stacking scheme, saying she “knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent.”

Her campaign has also denied any involvement in the matter.

articles.title: This election, trust the candidate that dares to touch Social Security
articles.summary: If candidates take benefit cuts off the table — or if they insist on taking taxes off the table, they are not leading; they are misleading you.
articles.body:
We’re told every election cycle that this one will be the most consequential of our lifetimes. But for the more than 70 million Americans who rely on Social Security, this election really does matter — because senators elected this November will need to save Social Security before their terms are up.

For an issue this important, the silence thus far is unnerving.

Every year the Social Security Trustees issue a report warning about the program’s impending fiscal cliff — now slated for 2032 , just six years away. Starting in that year, the Social Security Trust Fund will be exhausted, and annual payroll tax revenue will cover only 78 percent of promised benefits. The Trustees have issued this warning for decades. You would think our elected leaders would have done something by now to avoid the cliff.

Yet, year after year the president and Congress ignore the Trustee’s warning. Why?

The answer is simple, but sad. Our leaders will not lead. For their part, Democrats have largely refused to consider any restraint on the program’s costs. Meanwhile, Republicans have largely refused to consider revenue to cover those costs. With a few exceptions — such as recent stirrings among Republicans suggesting an openness to changing the payroll tax cap — both sides remain opposed to compromise.

In 1983, I was in my first term in Congress — actually in my first weeks on the job — and Social Security was in a crisis with less money flowing in than flowing out. Sadly, then, like now, politicians waited until the last minute to fix the problem.

The solution we enacted combined benefit restraint with additional revenue. We increased the retirement age gradually from 65 to 67. In addition, we accelerated payroll tax increases alongside higher taxes on wealthy retirees. Those changes were expected to maintain solvency in the Social Security system for 75 years.

But the projections were wrong. They were too optimistic in certain ways, such as fertility rates and wage growth. Since 2010 , Social Security has faced annual cash shortfalls, drawing down its reserves to pay full benefits.

Social Security’s Trustees now project this fundamental imbalance between the program’s costs and its revenues to continue, and to grow. Very soon, these deficits will exhaust the program’s reserves. Instead of maintaining solvency until 2058, as hoped, we are facing a serious shortfall in 2032.

Again, politicians are waiting until the last minute. Then, like now, the fix will require both reducing costs and adding revenue. And waiting carries a measurable cost. For example, the oft-cited solution to eliminate the payroll tax cap could have closed the 75-year solvency gap if enacted in 1995. Now, it would close two thirds of the gap .

The cost of delay is made even worse when you consider there really is no shortage of options to restore solvency to the Social Security System. Among the many options out there are extending the payroll tax to higher income levels, linking the retirement age to longevity, capping cost-of-living-adjustments for wealthier retirees or offering a flat rate adjustment . You can even try fixing the program yourself using interactive reform simulations . In doing so, you will learn that there is no easy, pain-free fix.

The bottom line is that waiting longer only makes matters worse.

That is why this election matters so much. The future of Social Security is very much on the ballot this year. Regardless of party, Americans deserve to know what our leaders are planning to do to avoid an unacceptable outcome. How candidates talk about this will be telling.

First and foremost, be wary of politicians who say they will not touch Social Security. If they won’t touch it, they can’t fix it.

Be skeptical too of politicians who claim they will protect your Social Security without saying how. Protecting Social Security requires some tough choices about costs and revenues. Everything has to be on the table. If candidates take benefit cuts off the table — or if they insist on taking taxes off the table, they are not leading; they are misleading you.

Protecting Social Security is a nice slogan. But it is not a solution.

Tim Penny is a co-chair of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. He represented Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1982 to 1994.
