articles.title: Texas' red wall facing its biggest threat in decades as Republicans scramble to defend it
articles.summary: James Talarico raised over $146 million for the Texas Senate race while Elon Musk bankrolled more than $200 million in outside support for Paxton.
articles.body: DALLAS — Democrats see a rare opening in Texas, and James Talarico is giving them their clearest shot in years at turning the state blue. If he pulls off the upset, the former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian could knock the first brick loose in Texas’ red wall. The polling and fundraising figures help explain why Democrats see that possibility. To put it in perspective, Talarico’s polling leads are wider than those recorded against Ted Cruz in 2018, when Beto O’Rourke came closer than any Democrat in decades to winning a Texas Senate race. And the enthusiasm on the ground from those who spoke with Fox News Digital backs up the numbers. DEEP IN TRUMP COUNTRY, A NEW GENERATION REVEALS THE DIVIDE BEHIND TEXAS’ TIGHT SENATE RACE What's more, Talarico’s campaign raised $64 million from July through September, more than three times Trump-backed candidate Ken Paxton’s $18 million haul over the same period. Since launching his campaign, Talarico has raised more than $146 million. But Paxton, currently the state's attorney general, has enjoyed Republican outside groups pouring more than $200 million into Texas to support him, nearly all of it bankrolled by Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. Additionally, MAGA Inc., President Donald Trump’s principal super PAC, has spent another $33.7 million on ads backing Paxton, according to AdImpact. At his Dallas rally on Thursday, Talarico underscored that divide by casting the race as a David and Goliath fight, telling supporters they were his weapon against powerful interests. "David wasn’t as big or as strong as Goliath. He didn’t have as many weapons, but he had hope. He had faith, and he had a slingshot," he said. "Dallas, you are my slingshot. The people of Texas are my slingshot." Talarico's momentum has also shown up on the campaign trail. 'That’s a lot of Talafreakos in one room' Earlier this week, Talarico hopscotched across Texas, stopping in El Paso before holding events in Midland and Amarillo and drawing a larger-than-expected crowd in deep-red Lubbock on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trump campaigned with Paxton about four miles away that same night, shifting his rally time so it overlapped with Talarico’s event. The dueling rallies put the race’s divide on display. Talarico’s campaign said more than 4,000 people signed up for his Lubbock rally, prompting a move to a larger venue. "I know that we’re not the only show in town tonight, and I appreciate all 4,000 of you that showed up here this evening," Talarico said at the Fiesta Center in Lubbock on Oct. 27. "That’s a lot of Talafreakos in one room." The Democratic candidate and his supporters have embraced the moniker "Talafreako," a nickname first given to him as a derogatory dig by Republicans and President Trump. Voters at Talarico’s rallies in Lubbock told Fox News Digital that Trump’s repeated Texas visits signaled Republican anxiety, while Paxton backers remained confident the state would stay red after a costly and contentious primary that saw Republicans divided over Paxton and sitting Sen. John Cornyn, who was ultimately ousted in the May runoff. "Trump’s in Lubbock? Trump’s in Lubbock, Texas? He’s scared, he is scared," one supporter told Fox News Digital. Natalie, from Friona, called Trump’s same-day rally a sign Republicans were "nervous." "I think it’s performative, like to come the exact same day as he is here," she said. Jenny, from Brownsville, told Fox News Digital outside Trump and Paxton's rally that the race was "not close" and she predicted that "Paxton will wipe the floor" with Talarico. DUELING RALLIES THRUST DEEP-RED LONE STAR TOWN INTO THE CENTER OF THE POLITICAL UNIVERSE Beyond the rally crowds, some Talarico supporters in Dallas and Lubbock said Paxton’s past legal controversies and impeachment by the Texas House shaped their views of the Republican nominee. "We’re here in support of honesty, decency and integrity," Lori, a Dallas voter who has voted Republican in the past, told Fox News Digital. "That’s what we like to see in a candidate, and we think Talarico is all that in one." George, a lifelong Texan at the Dallas rally, said years of watching Texas politics had become "heartbreaking" and called Talarico "a breath of fresh air." In Lubbock, Georgia cited several of Talarico’s policies and called him "authentic." She also said his lack of an indictment was a plus, contrasting him with Paxton. MEET THE VOTERS WHO COULD BREAK THE GOP’S DECADES-LONG GRIP ON A REPUBLICAN STRONGHOLD Elias, a nurse from Lubbock, described Paxton as a weak leader."He had a chance to kind of redeem himself despite his ugly past, but he’s not a man, he can’t stand up for himself. He needs daddy Trump to come and support him." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With Election Day on Nov. 3, the question is whether Talarico can turn rally crowds and a polling lead into a historic win. A victory would crack the GOP’s decades-long grip on Texas. A loss would leave Democrats still searching for a path to turn the state blue.

articles.title: Marshall says Trump dropping Kansas rally because he is ‘doing so well in the polls’
articles.summary: Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R) is defending President Trump’s decision to cancel his rally in the state, saying he can win without a visit from the president. “I think that I’m doing so well in the polls that he’s got, probably got better places to spend his time,” Marshall told reporters Thursday when asked for…
articles.body:
Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R) is defending President Trump’s decision to cancel his rally in the state, saying he can win without a visit from the president.

“I think that I’m doing so well in the polls that he’s got, probably got better places to spend his time,” Marshall told reporters Thursday when asked for his reaction to the president canceling his visit to the Sunflower State.

President Trump has not announced new rallies after he canceled his in-person rallies in Kansas and Iowa, and his last remaining scheduled in-person rally this campaign season is Friday in Florida. He’s opting to do tele-rallies for the rest of his midterm campaigning instead.

The Republican National Committee cited Republicans’ “strong position” in both states when explaining the cancellations.

Recent polls suggest Marshall may not be in a strong position for reelection, even in a state Trump won by more than 15 points in 2024. Three polls of the race released this week show Democrat Adam Hamilton leading Marshall. CNN/SSRS had Hamilton up by 4 points, The Washington Post/George Mason University showed him up by 10 and an Emerson College poll had Hamilton ahead by 3.5 points.

The Sunflower State has not elected a Democrat to the upper chamber in nearly 100 years, though it has elected Democrats for other statewide positions and currently has a Democratic governor, Laura Kelly.

The impact of Trump administration policies may be especially pronounced in a rural and farming-heavy state like Kansas. The Iran war has sent the price of diesel fuel skyrocketing , hovering at an average of $6.32 per gallon nationally and $6.03 per gallon in Kansas, according to AAA.

Driving Hamilton’s lead could be Trump’s approval rating — the Emerson poll found that 51 percent of Kansas likely voters disapproved of the president’s job performance, while 45 percent approved. Marshall’s vote share matched the share of voters who approved of Trump almost exactly in the survey.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, now gives Marshall just a 58 percent chance to win reelection, after giving him as high as a 90 percent chance earlier in the cycle.

Overall, DDHQ narrowly forecasts a Democratic Senate majority, giving the party a 60 percent chance to flip the chamber.

articles.title: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put 2 Dan Sullivans on ballot
articles.summary: Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters by recruiting Dan J Sullivan to also stand in the race.
articles.body:
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied she knew anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the Alaska Senate race.

The denial comes as the Trump administration continues to escalate a criminal investigation into the matter, according to US media. The Republican governor of the state ordered an official inquiry earlier this week.

Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.

The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.

"I just want to clear the air," Peltola said while speaking to voters on Thursday. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."

Both Dan Sullivans have been running for the open Senate seat for some time. Still, controversy erupted earlier this week when The New York Times reported that Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.

The Times's report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand in the Senate race.

The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.

The Peltola campaign has denied those reports and Sullivan has denied any links to the campaign.

But those denials have not stopped the justice department (DOJ) and Republicans from attacking Peltola.

The DOJ has begun issuing subpoenas targeting Democratic officials allegedly connected to the effort to recruit Dan J Sullivan to be on the Alaska ballot, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.

No charges had been filed as of Friday morning.

Scott Kendall, an attorney who worked with Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski in her 2010 and 2016 campaigns, told the BBC he was sceptical the actions described in the New York Times story broke the law.

Alaska law does not have specific good-faith requirements for candidates, Kendall explained - noting that spoiler candidates sometimes emerged in their contests.

"I freely admit there could be more facts, but I'm not going to speculate they exist," he said.

Kendall also said he believes the primary risk to Peltola from the allegations is "absolute reputational harm".

The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.

On Wednesday, the justice department amended its lawsuit to include the reporting by the Times, citing significant sections of the story as well as Governor Mike Dunleavy's announcement of an investigation.

A federal judge has expedited consideration and will weigh motions to dismiss brought by Alaska election officials and backed by the Peltola campaign and voting rights groups.

The legal action comes days before voters across the US head to the polls. This race in Alaska is among the closest-watched in the country, as it could be the deciding factor in who controls the Senate.

The non-partisan Cook Political Report currently classifies the race as a toss-up.

As the final weekend of campaigning approaches, President Donald Trump will appear at back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday.

The in-person appearances were previously cancelled, but a source familiar with planning told the BBC that they were rescheduled to accommodate remote appearances by Trump at tele-rallies.

articles.title: Progressives must show parents their vision for home-based childcare
articles.summary: Right now, the voices speaking most clearly to the desire for at-home care are pronatalist and regressive, favoring traditional gender hierarchies to grow the population at all costs.
articles.body:
Real momentum is building around efforts to reform our country’s childcare system, which parents have told policymakers is too costly and inaccessible for the vast majority of American working families.

New York City just announced a new program that will provide free childcare to more than 10,000 children. Less than a year ago, New Mexico became the first state to offer universal, no-cost childcare regardless of family income.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) recently introduced the Free Child Care for America Act , one of many 2028 hopefuls signaling their support for a universal childcare platform. National polling shows that more than 80 percent of parents nationwide support more federal funding for childcare.

The continued success of this movement will be decided on cultural terrain. There is plenty of data that shows how beneficial accessible childcare is to families. However, how families care for their children isn’t just a policy issue informed by evidence. Childcare touches on the most intimate elements of family wellbeing, and those who want to expand it must navigate the complex narratives swirling on this issue if they want to build durable support.

Right now, the voices speaking most clearly to the desire for at-home care are pronatalist and regressive, favoring traditional gender hierarchies to grow the population at all costs. That is a problem, because these efforts will only benefit a small, privileged sliver of society. Progressives cannot get boxed out on this issue.

Our organization, the FrameWorks Institute , has been studying the cultural mindsets that shape Americans’ understanding of child and family issues. Our research shows that engaging in policy conversations about children without the ability to see and navigate entrenched narratives and prevailing mindsets about parenting, children, gender and whose responsibility it is to care for kids, can stall long-term progress for families.

Ensuring childcare solutions respond to the realities and needs of families is key. There is mounting evidence that not all parents want center-based care, especially for infants. A new survey of 4,306 New York City parents and caregivers by the Robin Hood Foundation and New America’s New Practice Lab suggests that many parents want something different. Only 13 percent favored center-based programs for infants.

Much of the discussion about this topic in New York and elsewhere is focused on childcare centers and not enough on home care, despite the fact that large numbers of families use these care options, and they are closing at a disturbing rate . Home care is disproportionately used by working class families and families of color. For millions of U.S. families, home care settings are more convenient and offer more comfort and peace of mind than centers.

Creating solutions will require bipartisan consensus. Conservatives talk about home care often and are speaking to this need in a way that makes many parents feel heard.

We’ve watched pronatalist leaders like Vice President Vance make home-based care a centerpiece of conservative family policy, arguing that the government should reward people for having multiple children, for women staying at home to care for them and for public support going only to those raising kids within marriage . A new website launched by the Trump administration, called Moms.gov , echoes this rhetoric.

Childcare advocates must not let pronatalists own the conversation on in-home care. When pronatalists control the in-home care narrative, it becomes increasingly acceptable for benefits to be tied to marital status which, because marriage rates differ sharply by income and race , channels resources disproportionately to higher-income and white households, leaving out single-parent and low-income families.

Home-based childcare needs to be front and center for progressives like New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, or else they risk alienating many caregivers and ceding this ground. It’s a problem if Trump is perceived as making it easier to care for babies at home, and progressives are seen as creating barriers to this form of care or not mentioning it at all.

It’s not that Mamdani and other leaders are totally leaving home care out of their policy plans, but rather that they aren’t including this type of care when they are out talking about child and family wellbeing. Leaders should go out of their way to prioritize home care — in their policies and their communications. Doing so shows that they understand what families want and are doing what they can to meet their needs.

A childcare scale-up built around classroom seats and enrollment slots overlooks those who rely on grandparents, neighbors and licensed family childcare providers, especially in immigrant neighborhoods and communities of color. A childcare system that works requires prioritizing care in the settings families choose.

The growing momentum around childcare is creating real opportunities for change. If the pronatalist movement is left to dominate the narrative around in-home care, we will end up with a system designed for the families of some mythic past rather than those who exist right here, right now in this country.

If we want what’s happening in New York City to succeed and cascade to other parts of our nation, our policies — and our narratives — must reflect the full range of childcare options that families need.

Moira O’Neil is senior vice president of programs and Nat Kendall-Taylor is chief executive officer at the FrameWorks Institute.

articles.title: Dem operative admits Ilhan Omar case has legs as liberal firewall begins to crack: 'I'm not stupid'
articles.summary: A prominent Minnesota Dem operative says the federal investigation into Ilhan Omar's marriage fraud allegations is "almost certainly" legitimate.
articles.body: A prominent Minnesota Democrat who served in the state's House of Representatives revealed on Thursday he believes the federal probe into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has legitimacy. It's the latest signal that the political dam may be breaking as scandals and investigations into the congresswoman continue to pile up. "Democrats should understand that the allegation is almost certainly true—whatever conclusion they draw from that point could vary—and her denials calling it a right-wing, Islamophobic or racist conspiracy are almost certainly not," Joe Radinovich posted on X in reference to the claims that Omar married her brother as part of an alleged fraudulent immigration scheme. Radinovich, who served as a Minnesota state representative from 2013 to 2015 as a member of the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL), added to his post that, in addition to the probe into her immigration status, the investigation into her finances could also be problematic. OBAMA ADMIN FIRST LAUNCHED THE INVESTIGATION INTO ILHAN OMAR'S ALLEGED BROTHER MARRIAGE "And then I’d be very, very careful about how I qualified on allegations around her finances—where her defense looks similar and where no meaningful questions have been answered publicly, and where any objective look at the evidence doesn’t look…great," the former state representative said. Radinovich, a well-connected DFL operative with ties to the party’s state, federal and Minneapolis political establishments, managed Democrat Rick Nolan’s 2016 congressional campaign, ran Jacob Frey’s successful 2017 campaign for Minneapolis mayor and later served as Frey’s chief of staff. He also won the DFL nomination for Minnesota’s 8th Congressional District in 2018 before losing to Republican Pete Stauber. Briana Rose Lee, a Minneapolis DFL activist who served as an operations director for Omar’s campaign operation, responded to the post calling it a "witch hunt." "Joe. You aren’t stupid," she wrote. "You know this is a baseless and manufactured witch hunt. I’m actually surprised to see this from you. It’s a new low." NEARLY 40 HOUSE DEMS SKIP EFFORT TO END ILHAN OMAR IMMIGRATION PROBE Radinovich stood by his comments. "You’re right," Radinovich wrote. "I’m not stupid. I believe the Trump DOJ has next to no credibility and that it’s unclear to me the timing of the raid was appropriate—though it’s notable a DC judge signed off on it—but I’m pretty confident this specific allegation is true." Notably, Radinovich had a hand in two Democratic primary challenges against Omar, working with candidate Don Samuels in 2022 and 2024. Samuels lost both bids. Radinovich’s post is the latest example of the scrutiny surrounding Omar’s legal issues not being confined to conservative media or the MAGA base. Outlets including the New York Times, MSNBC, NBC News and The Associated Press have reported on evidence suggesting Omar’s marriage and citizenship may have been fraudulent, although no criminal charges have been filed against the Minnesota congresswoman. Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) on Oct. 12, 2026. HSI is the chief investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Her passport, phone and computer were seized during the early-morning operation. Fox News later reported that investigators are in possession of Omar's DNA. Omar's sister, Sahra Noor, voluntarily submitted to questioning shortly after the raid, skipping out on her book tour for a "family emergency." Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that the raid stemmed from an investigation into whether Omar or her late father, Nur Mohamed, fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork decades ago. The investigation, the sources noted, could lead to the congresswoman's denaturalization. But questions about whether Omar allegedly married her brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, in a fraudulent immigration scheme have also arisen. Omar has been plagued by the accusation for a decade, since she first ran for Minnesota state representative in 2016. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Court filings from the U.S. Attorney's Office in the District of Columbia referred to Omar as "Ilhan Omar Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Omar," suggesting that she shares a surname with the man she married in 2009. Ahmed Nur Said Elmi is a British citizen. Sources later told Fox News Digital that Ilhan Omar is not the Somali-born congresswoman's "real name." Omar's office has consistently denied the immigration fraud allegation, characterizing it as a right-wing smear. Most recently, she has said that the renewed scrutiny is the product of a political "vendetta" by President Donald Trump. But Thursday, Fox News Digital confirmed that former President Barack Obama's administration opened a probe into the allegedly fraudulent marriage in 2016. One source told Fox News Digital that the investigation remained open until 2021, when it was closed by the Biden administration. The Times reported that investigators believed the statute of limitations on a potential crime had passed. Omar's campaign attacked Radinovich in a Friday morning comment to Fox News Digital. "Joe is a deeply troubled individual whose demons have sadly manifested as an irrational obsession with Congresswoman Omar after managing two losing campaigns against her," the campaign said. "His claims are false, biased, and without any evidence. While he was once seen as a rising star within the party, Joe is now widely recognized as a shill for Republican and Corporate money."

articles.title: DOJ subpoenas California officials in voter rolls investigation escalation
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) has issued subpoenas to California officials in its latest move in scrutinizing voters in the state who aren’t U.S. citizens. Three subpoenas were sent to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder, ordering them to appear in court on Nov. 4, The Associated Press reported. Earlier this month, the…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) has issued subpoenas to California officials in its latest move in scrutinizing voters in the state who aren’t U.S. citizens.

Three subpoenas were sent to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder, ordering them to appear in court on Nov. 4, The Associated Press reported .

Earlier this month, the DOJ sued California after providing state and local election officials with a USB drive containing voter roll citizenship data, giving the state 48 hours to compare 20,000 names the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) flagged as noncitizens with its own data. The department sent a letter to the officials, which included a handwritten password to access the files on the thumb drive.

The subpoenas are requesting documents and communications related to letters sent to state election officials in July and October on allegations of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls, according to the AP. They are also seeking information about any efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted.

A DOJ spokesperson told The Hill the department “does not comment on leaks about alleged grand jury subpoenas.”

“The district court judge explained that voting unlawfully results in criminal exposure. Consistent with this, California also wrote in its filing that the remedy for unlawful voting is through criminal prosecution. Thus, while DOJ maintains that a civil remedy is still available, all agree that noncitizen voting is properly addressed through criminal law,” the spokesperson added.

President Trump, in a Truth Social post earlier this month, warned California officials that they could face criminal charges if they include the mail-in ballots from noncitizen voters.

In July, Trump alleged California, along with three other states, collectively had 250,000 noncitizens on their voter rolls. A federal “preliminary review” of these lists, which the DHS included in a letter sent to the states at the time, found less than half that number — 118,000 — matched the government had flagged.

Along with California, Washington state has also come under scrutiny in recent days, with federal officials calling on the state’s election officials to set aside ballots from more than 400 people who have allegedly registered to vote without U.S. citizenship.

Federal law dictates that only U.S. citizens are permitted to vote in federal elections, according to a fact sheet from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

articles.title: The middle powers step in, to America’s detriment
articles.summary: Last week, British Typhoon aircraft escorted French Rafale multirole fighters in a first-ever Anglo-French airborne nuclear strike exercise, codenamed Exercise Rummy. My former boss, Donald Rumsfeld, would not have been amused; it did not include American forces. Instead, as London stated, the exercise “mark[ed] a major step forward in UK-France defence cooperation under the [2025] Northwood…
articles.body:
Last week, British Typhoon aircraft escorted French Rafale multirole fighters in a first-ever Anglo-French airborne nuclear strike exercise , codenamed Exercise Rummy. My former boss, Donald Rumsfeld, would not have been amused; it did not include American forces. Instead, as London stated , the exercise “mark[ed] a major step forward in UK-France defence cooperation under the [2025] Northwood Declaration” to coordinate their nuclear deterrent strategies.

In fact, the joint effort was yet another indication of the increasing number of hedges on the part of what Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has termed “middle powers” against the possibility of America turning its back against its allies.

France has extended “forward deterrence” to ten European states — among them nuclear-armed Britain, with which, as the exercise demonstrated, there already exists a framework for nuclear cooperation. The French arrangement provides for joint exercises, such as the recently completed exercise with Britain; possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation among them.

None of these states has openly acknowledged that their cooperation is a hedge against American refusal to implement Article Five of the NATO Treaty in the event of a Russian attack. Yet the intent is obvious. As Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere put it , “we are doing this in light of the security policy situation in Europe, including Russia’s massive rearmament, also in the nuclear domain, and that it is waging a full-scale war against another European country.”

If Norway, and the other nine states were fully confident that America would come to their aid in the event of a Russian attack, why would they align themselves with a separate French nuclear deterrent?

The Europeans are not alone in expanding their hedges against an inward-looking America. On the same day as the British and French were conducting their exercise, Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar and Indonesia signed the “Badr Memorandum.” The memorandum provides for building on current military projects through joint production, technology transfer, and integrated supply chains. Although not a defense treaty, it could be a major step towards one — especially as two of the signatories, Turkey and Pakistan, recently did sign a defense treaty, the Mecca Defense Alliance, with Saudi Arabia.

The Saudis continue to suffer from Houthi attacks on their military and petroleum infrastructure. The Mecca treaty in some respects formalizes the support that both Pakistan and Turkey are already providing the Kingdom. Pakistan has aircraft and troops stationed in Saudi Arabia, whereas Turkey is furnishing planning support, logistics assistance, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance data, and support for drone and counter-drone operations.

It is noteworthy that other middle powers, both within and outside the region, are also aiding the Saudis. London announced that it would deploy Typhoon fighters to the Kingdom to help protect critical infrastructure and cities from Houthi attacks. French president Emmanuel Macron announced that France would deploy troops and air defense systems to help protect the Saudi port of Yanbu. And the Egyptian parliament approved sending military support to the Saudis.

Washington has thus far limited its aid to the Saudis, despite their entreaties for direct strikes on the Houthis. So the middle powers have stepped in, although they have limited their support to defending Saudi facilities and cities. None are likely to forget that it was they, and not the U.S., that came to the aid of the beleaguered kingdom.

As a former Pakistani prime minister once explained when I asked why it was to China, and not to the U.S., that Pakistan would first turn, he replied “the United States is a fair-weather friend, but China is an all-weather friend.” By leaving the Saudis to their own devices, Washington is not only pushing the middle powers to hedge their bets, it is also widening the door that the region has already opened to China.

This hedging on American support is not restricted to Europe and the Middle East. South Korea in particular is questioning its own previously tight relations with Washington.

President Trump’s threat of up to 300 percent tariffs on foreign companies that fail to build factories in the U.S. has been a source of friction between the two countries. Koreans also worry about the U.S. commitment to their country’s defense. It is noteworthy that more than three-fourths of the country’s population support South Korea developing its own nuclear weapons capability — a sentiment that Seoul may not be able to ignore indefinitely.

Winston Churchill famously remarked that “there is only one thing worse than fighting with allies, and that is fighting without them.” Washington should take note of Churchill’s aphorism, to forestall having the middle powers that are its allies today conclude that there is no point in remaining allies tomorrow.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

articles.title: Trump’s in-person rallies in Kansas, Iowa back on
articles.summary: President Trump will hold in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas after all, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill. The Thursday announcement that he would shift to tele-rallies in the battleground states stirred speculation about the president’s reason for scaling back his midterm travel schedule. The rallies were rearranged for scheduling purposes in…
articles.body:
President Trump will hold in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas after all, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill.

The Thursday announcement that he would shift to tele-rallies in the battleground states stirred speculation about the president’s reason for scaling back his midterm travel schedule.

The rallies were rearranged for scheduling purposes in an effort to accommodate dozens of additional tele-rallies recently added to the president’s schedule, the source said.

The Kansas rally was initially scheduled for Saturday and Iowa for Sunday. Both will now be held on Sunday.

The Republican National Committee said Thursday that the change in Trump’s plans would allow him to have a wider audience in the final days by holding more tele-rallies for candidates across the country.

The initial move was seen as a major reversal in strategy from Trump and his GOP allies, who have put on dozens of in-person rallies featuring Trump and Vice President Vance.

Trump snapped at a reporter on Thursday for asking him whether the change was because the president was sick of traveling.

“You’re sick to ask that question,” Trump said, going on to insult the reporter’s appearance.

Iowa and Kansas are seen as key midterm battlegrounds where Republicans have appeared to lose ground this election cycle as a result of disapproval of Trump and his handling of the economy.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated both races as toss-ups.

A CNN poll released Thursday showed incumbent Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R) trailing Democrat Adam Hamilton by 4 points, while an Emerson College/The Hill poll released earlier this month showed Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) leading Democrat Josh Turek by 2 points.

Both races have consistently polled within the margin of error.

articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV requested a mail ballot from Vatican City to vote in Illinois' midterm elections, potentially the first pope to vote in a U.S. election.
articles.body: American-born Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope ever to vote in a U.S. election. The Holy See Press Office confirmed to Fox News Digital on Friday that Leo, born Robert Francis Prevost and the first American-born pope in the Catholic Church's more than 2,000-year history, submitted a mail-in ballot in Illinois. "Pope Leo XIV has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See Press Office said. "The Holy See Press Office confirms that in keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago." "The Holy Father has also confirmed that, during his years of residence in Peru he exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so," the press office added. "The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes." CHICAGO'S 12-LANGUAGE BALLOTS MAKE ELECTIONS 'HARDER TO MONITOR,' ILLINOIS GOP CHAIR WARNS A spokesperson for the Will County clerk's office told Fox News Digital that "Robert Prevost is on the list of individuals who requested a Vote by Mail ballot." "Robert Francis Prevost is on the list of individuals who requested a vote by mail ballot for the upcoming election," Kim Fladhammer, Will County clerk’s office chief of staff, told the Chicago Sun-Times. Among the races on Illinois' ballot is the contest for governor, where incumbent Democrat J.B. Pritzker is seeking a third term against Republican Darren Bailey and independent candidate Collin Corbett. Pritzker's campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. POPE LEO XIV SEEN FOR FIRST TIME SINCE LUNG CANCER SURGERY AMID MAJOR RECOVERY MILESTONE "There is no such thing as an absentee ballot in Illinois law anymore. So anyone can vote by mail if they so choose. There is also a law called UOCAVA, The Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act that is mostly for the military, but it’s also for U.S. citizens who are overseas," Illinois State Board of Elections spokesman Matt Dietrich told the Chicago Sun-Times. "... Any Illinois registered voter can vote by mail." "Until 2010, it was considered absentee, and you had to have an excuse," Dietrich added. "But that’s all gone away. So that’s obviously what he’s doing." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Vatican announced on Oct. 13 that Leo underwent a procedure at Agostino Gemelli University Hospital in Rome to remove a small tumor on his right lung. Leo’s doctors later confirmed on Oct. 21 that no further cancer treatment is necessary after the pontiff’s lung tumor was removed.

articles.title: Chris Sununu: ‘Texas is in trouble for Republicans’
articles.summary: Former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu (R) is predicting doom for Republicans in the Texas Senate race, even as he maintains a more optimistic picture for his party nationally. Speaking with NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo on Thursday night, Sununu predicted that Republican Ken Paxton would lose to Democrat James Talarico in Texas next week. “I think…
articles.body:
Former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu (R) is predicting doom for Republicans in the Texas Senate race , even as he maintains a more optimistic picture for his party nationally.

Speaking with NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo on Thursday night, Sununu predicted that Republican Ken Paxton would lose to Democrat James Talarico in Texas next week.

“I think Texas is in trouble for Republicans,” Sununu said on “Cuomo.”

No Democrat has won a Senate race in Texas since the 1980s , but the party thinks it has a good shot this year due to Paxton’s weaknesses as a candidate.

Aside from the Lone Star State’s race, the former New Hampshire governor maintains a much more optimistic picture of the Senate than some in his party, as he predicted that “extremists” will lose.

Sununu said he thought reported accusations of ballot stacking against Democrats in Alaska may help Republicans hold the seat, and he predicted wins for the GOP in Maine and Michigan, citing past polling misses .

“You have conservatives or Republicans that just don’t answer polls. They just don’t come out. So we’re always massively underpolled,” Sununu said.

Polls have underestimated Republicans in those states before, but that happened mainly in presidential years when President Trump was on the ballot. An analysis by political data analyst Nate Silver found that while polls significantly overstated Democrats’ leads in 2016, 2020 and 2024, the polls were nearly perfect, with errors of less than half a point, in 2018 and 2022 — the two most recent midterms.

If polls are to be believed this year, they predict an especially bad night for Republicans. According to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, Democrats trail in the average of polls in only two competitive Senate races — Iowa and South Carolina — and lead in all the others. That includes deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and Ohio.

Sununu dismissed polls showing competitive races in some of those states, saying Republicans will “be fine.”

“The conservative states, it’ll be close. But South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, they’ll be fine,” Sununu said.

Sununu’s brother, former Sen. John Sununu (R-N.H.), is on the ballot this year, running for his old seat in the Granite State against Rep. Chris Pappas (D). While some polls conducted after the September primary showed a close race, Pappas has since pulled ahead and leads by 7 points, according to DDHQ.

Overall, DDHQ’s forecast gives Democrats a 60 percent chance to take back control of the Senate.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV casts historic vote in US midterm election
articles.summary: The Chicago-born pontiff, who has a tense relationship with Trump, mailed in a ballot for the midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has submitted his mail-in ballot in Illinois, for the midterm elections, becoming the first-ever pope to vote in a US election.

"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Holy See Press Office said in a statement.

The Chicago-born pontiff is the first US citizen to hold the Vatican's highest seat, after his selection in May 2025.

Since then, he has clashed with the Trump administration over various issues, including immigration enforcement and the US-Israel war with Iran.

"Pope Leo XIV has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the press office said, including during his years in Peru.

The US midterm elections will determine which political party controls Congress and have a significant impact on the final years of Donald Trump's presidency.

Elections will be held nationwide on 3 November, but early voting has begun in most states.

According to NBC News, the Pope requested his mail-in ballot from the Will County Clerk's Office on 3 October.

Less than two weeks later, the Vatican announced he had surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung after he was diagnosed with lung cancer.

The Vatican confirmed last week that the Pope, aged 71, will travel as planned to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru in early November.

Tensions escalated between the Pope and the US president in April, after the Pope called for peace in the wake of US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

"I don't think he's doing a very good job," Trump said about the Pope afterwards.

"We don't like a Pope that's going to say that it's OK to have a nuclear weapon," he continued. "I'm not a big fan of Pope Leo."

Pope Leo followed with his own remarks later, saying: "The mission of the Church is to preach the Gospel, to preach peace," according to Reuters.

"If someone wants to criticise me for preaching the Gospel... I hope simply to be listened to because of the value of God's words."

In the final few days before the midterms, Republican and Democratic officials alike are sprinting across the country to boost their party's chances of success.

Polls suggest Democrats are the favourite to gain control of the lower chamber of Congress, called the House of Representatives, and are poised to win seats in Republican-leaning areas that overwhelmingly voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

Democrats also appear to have a chance to win additional seats in the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress.

The gloomy outlook for Trump's Republican party has seen the president hold several rallies in states where Republican victories are typically all but guaranteed.

articles.title: How one billionaire could ‘singlehandedly’ alter the course of the midterms
articles.summary: Elon Musk has plowed nearly half a billion dollars into elections in the 2026 cycle, a spending spree that makes him the single, largest disclosed donor in m...
articles.body:
Elon Musk has plowed nearly half a billion dollars into elections in the 2026 cycle, a spending spree that makes him the single, largest disclosed donor in modern American politics and one of the Republican Party's largest-ever benefactors.

The world's richest man has contributed more than $445 million to federal committees alone through mid-October – more than double the nearly $177 million that Democratic megadonor George Soros gave to outside groups during the 2022 cycle to become the largest known individual donor in the last midterm elections for Congress.

Musk's money could "single-handedly" alter the course of the midterms, said Brendan Glavin, who oversees research at the nonprofit OpenSecrets. The group tracks political spending.

"One person is completely dominating and changing the landscape of how Republicans are able to spend money and defend themselves," he said.

Musk has donated nearly $216 million to America PAC, the super PAC at the center of his political operation. The group's activity spans more than 40 House and Senate races this fall, according to federal campaign data.

But nowhere has the billionaire spent more than in Texas, where he lives and has headquartered parts of his business empire.

The key Senate contest there between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton could determine which party controls the chamber during the last two years of President Donald Trump's tenure in the White House.

America PAC has funded mailers, digital advertising and other outreach to Texas voters in an effort to defeat Talarico and other Democrats.

But far more Musk money – at least $168 million so far – has been deployed in Texas through other groups. A pair of donations last month, for instance, from the SpaceX CEO to the Senate Leadership Fund, a leading Republican super PAC, were quickly funneled to a second group, Texas PAC, that has issued blistering attacks against Talarico on the airwaves, recent disclosures show.

Much of the anti-Talarico messaging seeks to portray him as out of step with Texas values, with some citing his vote as a state legislator against a 2023 law banning gender surgeries and other medical interventions for minors. (Talarico's campaign has said he does not support gender surgery for children but opposed the bill because it was overly broad.)

Musk also has donated $10 million to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which as CNN's KFILE reported this week, has underwritten AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico.

A spokesperson for Musk's America PAC declined to comment.

But Republicans familiar with the strategy said the PAC is broadly focused on helping the GOP retain control of Congress next year and describe Musk's move to shoulder some of the Texas advertising costs as freeing other GOP groups to deploy resources elsewhere to protect the Senate majority.

In a statement, the Senate Leadership Fund's executive director Alex Latcham said the donors who stepped up to fund Texas PAC "ensured that we did not have to divert any resources from other key races" and have allowed the group "to run effective campaigns across the map."

Talarico has raised more money than any other federal candidate this cycle, $146 million through October 14, more than six times the $22.3 million collected by Paxton, according to Federal Election Commission records . And a CNN poll released Thursday shows the Democrat with a narrow lead over Paxton.

But Talarico has faced an onslaught of outside spending from pro-Paxton interests, including those funded by Musk, in recent weeks. In the final four weeks of the Texas Senate campaign, Democrats have been outspent by Republicans on ads by more than 2 to 1, $118.9 million to $54.7 million, according to AdImpact data.

Dave Carney, a top political adviser to Texas GOP Gov. Greg Abbott's reelection campaign, says Republicans in the state believe the spending by Musk and other GOP groups is starting to exact a toll on Talarico.

"It has taken the pretty boy, neighbor next door, cute moderate nice guy and has exposed his voting record," Carney told CNN this week.

Talarico is increasingly taking aim at Musk to highlight his outsized role in the Texas race, as Democrats work to motivate their voters to turn out in the final stretch.

"Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat," Talarico said during a recent rally as he ticked off the breadth of Musk-funded activity in the state.

"In all likelihood, if you've seen an attack ad on your TV, that was Elon," he said. "If you've gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you've received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon, too."

A recent digital ad from Talarico reinforced the message, saying Paxton "will owe him everything" if Musk's money helps to elect the Republican.

A Paxton spokesperson did not respond to CNN's inquiry.

Democrats have sought to use Musk as a foil to spur turnout before.

In Wisconsin last year, a $20 million spending blitz by Musk and aligned groups – along with his decision to campaign in the state – became a central message for Democrats who soundly defeated Musk's preferred candidate in a state Supreme Court contest.

Other Democratic ads that year used images of Musk holding a chainsaw aloft to highlight his controversial and short-lived tenure running the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency.

This year, Musk has kept a lower profile, even as his political spending has soared to new heights. He has not campaigned with candidates.

But he has used X, the social media platform he controls to amplify his criticism of Talarico with increasing frequency. In the last week, he's posted more than a dozen times about the Democrat, often disparaging him as "far-left extremist."

Musk and his spending loom large over the election, said Lynda Tran, a Democratic strategist based in Washington.

The billionaire may not be on stage "wielding a chainsaw and other theatrics," she said, "but there's no way to hide the ball on the contributions he's making or how much he cares about various Republican races."

CNN's David Wright contributed to this report.

articles.title: Drone warfare will be won at the operator level
articles.summary: Rather than building systems around individual platforms and asking operators to navigate between them, we should build around the operator.
articles.body:
We are witnessing modern warfare create a paradox. The battlefield has never had more intelligence, yet the soldier may have less time than ever to use it. A drone can be detected by one system, classified by another, tracked by a third and defeated by yet another. Each system may work as designed. But if those capabilities can’t converge around the person who has seconds to act, technological superiority becomes irrelevant.

It poses a fundamental and lethal gap for our warfighters.

Drone warfare will be won at the operator level. The advantage won’t belong to the military with the best drones or the most sophisticated interceptor, but to the military that brings intelligence and capability together around the individual solider, creating a decision advantage at machine speed.

For decades, military modernization has delivered extraordinary advances in sensing, communications and precision. But drone warfare exposes a dangerous weakness. A small aerial threat can emerge with little warning, leaving a soldier seconds to understand what’s happening and respond. The challenge isn’t simply whether information exists. It’s whether the person who needs it can understand it and act before it’s too late.

Information superiority doesn’t automatically translate into decision superiority. A warfighter surrounded by sensors and intelligence may still lack a clear picture of what to do next. More information can become a burden when every new capability introduces another stream of data demanding attention.

We have spent years putting more information in front of soldiers. Now we must remove the complexity. Militaries are developing increasingly capable electronic warfare systems. The challenge is making them work together.

Rather than building systems around individual platforms and asking operators to navigate between them, we should build around the operator — something like an Iron Dome for the individual. Sensors, autonomous assets and defensive capabilities should converge through a common coordination layer that absorbs technical complexity and presents the operator with a clear understanding of the threat and available options.

Agentic artificial intelligence could transform this process. Unlike AI that simply analyzes information, agentic systems can coordinate tasks and available tools. Such a system could process sensor data, classify a threat, identify available defensive capabilities and present options. The operator would no longer need to navigate multiple systems to understand what can be done.

The goal isn’t to show warfighters everything a machine knows. It’s to provide what they need to know when they need it. Machine speed should compress complexity while humans remain in charge.

Our perspectives come from different experiences. One of us spent two decades in Army Special Operations, including 18 combat deployments. Another has worked across government and emerging technology, focusing on artificial intelligence and systems design. And one of us investigated and uncovered dangerous flaws on the production line of one of the nation’s most complicated and important military aircraft.

Yet all these experiences point to the same principle: Battlefield technology should make the operator more capable, not irrelevant.

Such a system could give an individual soldier a tactical edge by coordinating capabilities that once required multiple interfaces or specialists. This wouldn’t eliminate command structures. It would create greater situational awareness and improve decision-making on the battlefield.

But it must work under battlefield conditions even when communications fail, GPS degrades and networks go down. Adversaries can manipulate information and attack the systems carrying it. Battlefield AI must be designed for degraded environments, enabling useful intelligence even when distant command centers or cloud connections are unavailable.

The Pentagon should also expand how it measures counter-drone performance. Detection range, interception probability, accuracy and cost remain important. But so does the time between detecting a threat and enabling a human response. A system that detects a drone earlier but complicates the decision-making process isn’t an operational advantage.

There are real risks. AI can misclassify threats, fail in unexpected conditions or encourage excessive trust in machine recommendations. These dangers are serious when lethal force is involved. The answer is not simply greater autonomy.

Human oversight must be built in. Operators need more than the ability to approve a final action; they need situational understanding and authority over decisions. AI should perform tasks that machines can execute faster while helping humans make better decisions under pressure.

The U.S. must stop asking only how much more technology it can put in warfighters’ hands. It must ask how much complexity it can remove. As drones proliferate and autonomy increases, the time available to make decisions shrinks. More sensors and interceptors won’t matter if operators can’t act quickly.

Drone warfare will be won by the military that connects its systems, compresses decision time and puts intelligence where it matters most: with the person whose life depends on it.

The goal of battlefield AI is not to remove the human from the fight. It is to give the human an advantage within it.

Thomas Payne is a recipient of the U.S. Army’s Medal of Honor for actions during his service in Iraq in 2015. Cesar R. Hernandez is a fellow at Harvard’s Kennedy School of Government, a developer at the MIT Media Lab, and an MBA graduate of Oxford University. Alan M. Cohn is a Peabody and Emmy Award-winning journalist.

articles.title: Leo XIV becomes first pope ever to vote in US general election
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election.
articles.body:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election .

The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of next week’s midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.

Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen” and has done so “whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Holy See press office said.

The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible.

“The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added.

Leo’s vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times , which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk’s office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3.

It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. His brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude’s, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Ill. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.

Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.

The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a ballot in a primary, when parties choose their nominees for the general election. No such declaration is required in general elections.

While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.

The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.

articles.title: The silent majority problem and why campaign pollsters keep 'fighting the last war' on elections
articles.summary: From Literary Digest's 1936 disaster to partisan polls skewing primaries, Tevi Troy traces 90 years of polling mishaps and why errors keep recurring.
articles.body: Ninety years ago, on Oct. 31, 1936, Literary Digest, which had correctly forecast presidential election winners since 1916, predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Delano Roosevelt in the upcoming election. Roosevelt won handily. The Digest’s poll surveyed 10 million people via postcard, using telephone books and car registration lists for the information. Even though almost 2.4 million people responded — an impressive response rate — the misleading sample provided inaccurate results. Literary Digest folded shortly afterward. Two years later, in 1938, Gallup started tracking presidential approval ratings. Even so, polls remained far from perfect. In 1948, the Chicago Daily Tribune’s embarrassing front-page declaration "Dewey Defeats Truman" stemmed in part from a misuse of polling. The paper relied on earlier polls that did not reflect the Election Day reality in making its prediction. As the science of polling improved over time, campaign pros began to rely on pollsters. John F. Kennedy was the first president to be strongly associated with a polling firm, as he used Lou Harris and the Harris organization's polls in his 1960 campaign for president. LEE CARTER: AMERICA IS ANGRY AT EVERYONE — BUT WHO WILL ACTUALLY VOTE? In the 1970s, we witnessed the rise of the celebrity pollsters: Pat Caddell for Jimmy Carter, Richard Wirthlin for Ronald Reagan, and Stan Greeberg and Dick Morris for Bill Clinton. These pollsters were successful but not infallible. Caddell, for instance, was largely responsible for Carter's 1979 "Crisis of Confidence" speech. He misjudged the public mood, and Carter’s "malaise speech" became one of the most disastrous presidential speeches of all time. Morris, for his part, had a tempestuous relationship with Bill Clinton. They once reportedly came to blows while Morris was advising Clinton during his time as governor of Arkansas. Morris was initially on the outs and Greenberg in charge of polls when Clinton won the 1992 election. But Morris secretly came back and started advising Clinton after the Democrats lost control of Congress in the 1994 "Republican Revolution." Morris even had a code name — "Charlie" — to keep his identity secret from the more liberal White House staff, which resented Morris’ pushing of Clinton to the center. Morris would poll everything, even where Clinton should go on vacation. When Clinton left office after two terms in 2000, he had survived the Monica Lewinsky scandal — despite polls showing that Americans strongly disapproved of Clinton's behavior. The most important number for Clinton was the Gallup approval rating. He left office at 66%, one of the highest outgoing figures in history. 21st-century presidents would be thrilled to get approval ratings anywhere near Clinton's final number. George W. Bush hit 86% after the 9/11 terror attacks, but that did not last. For the most part, the "low and steady" phenomenon has meant that presidents in this century have struggled to get about 50% approval. TRUMP VS HISTORY: HOW PRESIDENT'S POLL NUMBERS COMPARE TO BIDEN, OBAMA, BUSH AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Still, the polling mishaps have continued. In 2004, exit polls predicted a win for John Kerry over George W. Bush. Campaign adviser Bob Shrum even said to Kerry on Election Day, "Can I be the first to call you, Mr. President?" The exit polls were wrong, and Bush won a second term. In 2012, Mitt Romney’s campaign wrongly thought it was headed for victory when its pollster made overly optimistic weighting assumptions. The turnout model incorrectly assumed that Barack Obama would not generate the same level of youth and minority turnout that he had in 2008. LIZ PEEK: FIVE REASONS REPUBLICANS COULD DEFY THE POLLS AND SHOCK DEMOCRATS ON ELECTION DAY Polling took another big hit in 2016, when pollsters confidently predicted that Hillary Clinton would defeat Donald Trump. She didn't, and the pollsters’ justification that they had the popular vote right but got the election result wrong did not help matters. In our current midterm elections, we have seen a new wrinkle. Partisan polls overstated progressive support in the primaries, skewing the results and causing some candidates to drop out in the face of the inaccurate data. This latest mishap reinforces the lesson that polling often fails, although rarely in the same way twice. DEMOCRATS FURIOUS AFTER POLLSTER BOOSTING FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES ADMITS FABRICATING SURVEYS: ‘ABSOLUTE SCUMBAGS’ While technology and the science of polling are much better today than in 1936, the improvements complicate matters further. While nearly everyone has a phone, they also have caller ID and don't answer calls from unfamiliar numbers. Response rates shrink, increasing the size of the "silent majority." In this new environment, human modeling decisions ironically become more, not less, important. Polling errors come not from new techniques or technologies but from imperfect human decisions about how to deploy the new technologies. In making those decisions, pollsters can overreact to what went wrong beforehand. In this, pollsters are like generals, often fighting the last war. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In the end, polls are more accurate as snapshots of opinion rather than predictors of behavior, specifically, who will actually submit a ballot. This means that whatever the polls say, the public should be wary. To borrow from the Psalms, put not your trust in polls, and get out and vote.

articles.title: DOJ accuses Peltola, Democrats of misleading a federal court
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday accused Mary Peltola of misleading a federal court in the latest filing in its lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate election. “Apparently emboldened by the success of their reported plot to deceive Alaskan voters, Alaskans For Mary and the DSCC [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] appear…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday accused Mary Peltola of misleading a federal court in the latest filing in its lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate election.

“Apparently emboldened by the success of their reported plot to deceive Alaskan voters, Alaskans For Mary and the DSCC [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] appear to have turned to misleading this Court,” the amended complaint filed Thursday read.

“They orchestrated this sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected,” it added.

The DOJ’s lawsuit, initially filed last week, argues that the U.S. Senate election in Alaska will be invalid unless incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) wins amid voter confusion about a candidate with the same name as the incumbent also appearing on the ballot.

The latest filing cites The New York Times’s recent report that Peltola’s campaign was directly involved in recruiting someone with the same name as her opponent , the incumbent senator.

“Although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief,” the filing read. “It also aligns with common sense.”

Even if Peltola’s campaign did indeed recruit Dan J. Sullivan, the additional candidate, that action would not be against the law, Scott Kendall, an Alaskan lawyer and former GOP operative, told The Hill .

“These allegations don’t make the Department of Justice’s case a better case,” Kendall said. “There’s no basis for this lawsuit.”

Kendall said ballot-stacking “can be a nasty, dirty trick” and “there can be bad motives behind it, but according to our Alaska Supreme Court, which is empowered to interpret Alaska law, it is not illegal.”

The DOJ has also issued dozens of subpoenas in connection with the case, which have been sent to Peltola’s Senate campaign offices as well as the offices of Dan J. Sullivan.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) on Wednesday ordered an investigation into whether Peltola’s campaign violated state law in the alleged scheme. The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee also launched an investigation into the former Democratic lawmaker.

In a Truth Social post Wednesday, President Trump said Peltola should face legal and political consequences. He has also said Peltola should not be allowed to run for Senate after the allegations.

Peltola, on Thursday, denied any knowledge of the alleged ballot-stacking scheme, saying she “knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent.”

Her campaign has also denied any involvement in the matter.

The competitive race in Alaska leans narrowly in favor of the Democrat, whom nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives a 60 percent chance of winning.

articles.title: How ‘You Can See Everything’ unmasks our modern age of manufactured reality
articles.summary: We can see everything in “You Can See Everything,” but seeing is not the same as knowing. Fielder and Oppenheim’s film is so effective because it knows that too.
articles.body:
Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s “You Can See Everything” is a movie for our times — not only because it is the rare documentary with box office appeal and Oscar buzz , but because it strikes at something in the culture of this century that almost defies description.

The film centers on the Theranos debacle of the last decade and how someone like Elizabeth Holmes tries to repair a private and public life after being classified as one of the business world’s biggest frauds . But in a larger sense, it is also about the gnawing unease and increasing difficulty we are all experiencing in our own lives as we contend with today’s grift economy, in a world of diffuse media, algorithmic filter bubbles and infinite forums for people to speak their version of the truth.

“You Can See Everything” also homes in on the prized ethos of “fake it ‘til you make it” that now defines business and startup culture. Holmes was one of the most flagrant Steve Jobs clones , right up to the turtleneck, applying her brand of magical thinking to blood testing the way others did to apps or digital currencies or virtual worlds or artificial intelligence.

But what happens when such magical thinking extends to fraud, billions’ worth of investment , and the corruption of medicine , a field whose very foundation is “do no harm?” Or when your belief that a piece of technology might be able to deliver someday on what you are promising is not the same as actually being able to deliver today?

Yet Oppenheim and Fielder have no interest in a deep dive on the details of Theranos, as multiple news investigations, television shows and court proceedings already have undertaken. It is enough to have the movie turn on a single statement Holmes made to The New York Times in 2023, unlocking a heuristic for what might be fundamental dishonesty or fundamental confusion, as Fielder deploys a lethal narrowing of eyes and the most skeptical “OK” this side of Larry David.

Perhaps that figured into the calculus of Holmes to bring Fielder and Oppenheim into this sort of project in the first place. By limiting this embedded recording to a few weeks in a San Diego guest house, it might have been possible for Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, to play-act the image they wanted to create in the weeks leading up to Holmes’s incarceration. It’s essentially what some brands have been doing for decades in trying to shift the narrative — maybe we can call this docu-washing.

There is so much strangeness to what we see, though, that it is difficult to fathom what that attempt at manipulating image and discourse might have been.

Is Holmes really just a naif who might be on the spectrum and suffering from the PTSD of a sexual assault at Stanford , as well as the victim of a Svengali-like manipulation by the men in her life ?

Is Billy really losing his grip on reality because of what has happened to Holmes, or is it one more con designed to solicit money, sympathy or something else? Are his strong feelings for Charlie Kirk a result of red-pilling and being chronically online during Holmes’s incarceration, or is he cynically building a framework for a pardon from a pro-Kirk president ?

Are they both two very confused people still in love and trying to build a family, or are they just deeply embedded in characters they agreed to create for Holmes’s post-Theranos life?

Even amid the fascinating mystery swirling around Holmes and Evans, the second half of the film does not hesitate to interrogate post-Holmes media like “The Dropout,” which seems to have created its own version of reality “based on a true story.” Here, the focus turns to the media that did create a new Holmes character, cutting its own corners of the truth in an attempt to create a more compelling emotional reality.

Dramatic license is not medical malpractice, but when dealing with real people, it can also be its own form of bad faith. The great power of this film is that it does not just put Holmes, Evans and the associated grift economy under the microscope, but the grift economy’s outrage machine as well — and even the makers of the movie itself.

We can see everything in “You Can See Everything,” but seeing is not the same as knowing. Fielder and Oppenheim’s film is so effective because it knows that too.

Ian Chaffee is a technology and startup media relations consultant based in Los Angeles.

articles.title: Stevens to appear alongside El-Sayed for first time in months, but expects apology
articles.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) on Sunday will appear alongside Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for the first time in months in what appears to be a reluctant show of unity after criticizing the Democratic nominee for his comments about Israel. Stevens confirmed Friday in a statement posted to the social platform X that she would…
articles.body:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) on Sunday will appear alongside Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for the first time in months in what appears to be a reluctant show of unity after criticizing the Democratic nominee for his comments about Israel.

Stevens confirmed Friday in a statement posted to the social platform X that she would join Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.) and El-Sayed at a church service in Detroit this Sunday.

“I say this with no race to run and nothing to gain,” Stevens said. “The Jewish and African American communities of my district deserve to see their leaders show up for them rather than fight over them.”

A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment about the joint appearance or Stevens’s comments.

Stevens said she accepted the invitation to appear alongside El-Sayed from Clyburn, not from El-Sayed’s campaign.

The joint appearance comes after Stevens’s fiance revealed he would vote for El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), because of El-Sayed’s rhetoric about Israel.

Tension emerged over a digital ad run by an outside progressive group in which a woman is grocery shopping and appears to blame Israel for high prices . El-Sayed’s campaign previously said it was not responsible for the ad.

Stevens criticized the ad for “fearmongering” and told CNN on Wednesday that a lot of Michigan voters are “hurt” and “confused,” calling on El-Sayed to denounce the ad .

In her statement Friday, she again criticized her former primary opponent for not condemning the ad more forcefully, calling on the Democratic nominee to get “Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”

“The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care,” Stevens said. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.”

El-Sayed has been highly critical of Israel throughout the campaign, with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israel lobbying group, spending millions on behalf of Stevens in the primary. El-Sayed ultimately defeated Stevens by a narrow margin.

Rogers has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed for his comments about Israel and is courting disaffected Jewish voters , including Democrats. Polls show a competitive race, but one in which El-Sayed narrowly leads.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives El-Sayed a 73 percent chance to retain the seat for Democrats.
